news.title: United States of Dolly: How a country queen bridged America’s divide
news.text:
WASHINGTON - The death of country music icon Dolly Parton, who kept her distance from the political debates gripping America, offered a rare moment of unity to a divided nation on Aug 25.

Affording her the sort of honour given to major state figures, US President Donald Trump ordered flags across the country to be lowered for a week to mark what he called a “true loss for millions of people”.

And Trump spared the legendary singer – who like him was 80 – the kinds of barbs he has levelled at other figures including former FBI chief Robert Mueller and director Rob Reiner after their deaths.

Reactions to the death of the Jolene star were the same on the other side of the political divide.

“Dolly Parton was a true American icon,” said Kamala Harris, Trump’s Democratic rival in the 2024 US presidential election, and the first female and Black US vice-president.

Worried about its future and often nostalgic for an idealised past, it is fair to say that much of America saw itself in Dolly Parton.

Perhaps it was because the child who grew up in a cabin without running water or electricity in Tennessee, and became a global, successful businesswoman and generous philanthropist, reflected a flattering image back to the world’s leading power.

The queen of country music herself never got involved in politics, rising above the fact that the scene has frequently leaned conservative.

Parton repeatedly insisted that her songs said all she had to say.

“Everybody knows I don’t do politics,” she told Fox and Friends in 2017.

“My mother was a Democrat and my daddy was a Republican, so I’m a hypocrite,” she quipped.

Parton also said she had fans on both side of the aisle “and I don’t want to make any of them mad at me.”

‘All for gals’

A devout Christian, she also became a supporter of gay rights.

“We are all God’s children,” she said in an interview with Larry King in 2016.

In that same year, she also declined to say whether she would support either Democrat Hillary Clinton or Republican Trump in the presidential election.

Parton told The New York Times that “a woman would do a great job” but added that: “I think no matter if it’s Hillary or Donald Trump, we’re gonna be plagued with PMS either way – presidential mood swings!”

During the Covid pandemic, Parton waded into another politically charged area by funding vaccine research and encouraging Americans to get vaccinated. She even sang a parody version of her hit song Jolene, renamed Vaccine, while filming a video of her first injection.

But Parton, whose hit 9 To 5 was a feminist anthem, declined to describe herself as such despite shaking up the male dominated country music industry.

“I’m just all for gals,” she told The Guardian in 2019.

The result was a moment of almost unheard-of unity for a country split over everything from the Iran war to the culture wars.

While Trump did not mention it in his Truth Social post, there was widespread praise from both parties for her Imagination Library programme, which gave away millions of free books to children.

“She always believed in giving back, especially in her efforts to promote literacy,” said Democratic former president Bill Clinton.

Trump’s Education Secretary Linda McMahon concurred, saying Dolly Parton “placed millions of books into the hands of young children and helped spark a lifelong love of reading”.

The Democrats, however, could not resist pointing out that Trump’s Republicans had tried to reduce funding for Parton’s signature programme. AFP

news.title: Map Shows Congressional Races Now Toss-Ups in Districts Trump Won
news.text: The 2026 House map is showing new signs of potential vulnerability for Republicans, with races shifting toward Democrats in districts that President Donald Trump carried in the 2024 presidential election. The latest changes from the nonpartisan Cook Political Report include two races moving from “Lean Republican” to “Toss Up”—Florida’s 14th Congressional District and Michigan’s open 10th District. Michigan’s 8th District, meanwhile, pivoted from “Lean Democrat” to “Likely Democrat.” The shifts are notable because both Florida and Michigan backed Trump statewide in 2024. Trump won Florida with more than 6.1 million votes and carried Michigan with about 2.82 million votes, narrowly defeating former Vice President Kamala Harris in the swing state that had backed ex-President Joe Biden in 2020. The districts themselves also backed Trump in 2024, underscoring the potential significance of Cook's latest ratings. In Michigan, Trump carried the 10th by roughly 7 points and the 8th by about 2 points, Cook highlights. Newsweek reached out to the White House via email on Tuesday for comment. Why It Matters The three shifts highlight how the 2026 midterm landscape could put Republican incumbents under pressure even in districts that historically have been favorable to the GOP. Midterm elections are commonly seen as a measure of public approval for the current president too, and the president's party has traditionally lost seats during these elections. At present, Republicans maintain a narrow House majority, controlling 218 seats, while Democrats hold 212. With control of the House up for grabs in the upcoming midterm, even modest shifts in Democrats' favor could be consequential. What To Know Florida’s 14th District presents a particularly interesting test. The Tampa-area quadrant is represented by Democratic Representative Kathy Castor, but Cook previously rated the contest as Lean Republican following redistricting. The race is now considered a Toss Up after Florida’s primary elections established the November matchup and new information, including polling, gave Democrats a stronger position, Cook says. According to Cook's analysis, Trump would have won the newly redrawn district in 2024 by 11 percent. Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek on Tuesday, "The shift of Florida’s 14th from Lean Republican to toss up is notable but fits the broader pattern of ratings moving toward Democrats as the midterm environment hardens." Agranoff continued: "Redistricting made the seat more Republican on paper, with Trump carrying the new lines by double digits, so it does not lean Democratic in a structural sense. What it does show is that a well-established incumbent like Kathy Castor can still keep a redrawn district competitive when the national climate is difficult for the party in power. The other two moves in Michigan point in the same direction. This is less about any single Florida race flipping blue and more about how the map is responding to current political conditions." Michigan’s 10th District is also moving into Toss Up territory as an open seat. It includes parts of southeastern Michigan and does not have an incumbent seeking reelection after Representative John James left the House to run for governor. Trump won the district in 2024, making the increasingly competitive race another example of Democrats challenging Republicans in territory that favored the president just two years ago. The latest changes build on a broader pattern of movement across the 2026 House map, with Democrats aiming to seize on a political environment that has seemingly become more favorable to them as the midterms approach. Cook's ratings are not predictions of the final outcome, but rather assessments of the expected competitiveness of each race. With primary contests largely settled and general-election matchups taking shape, districts that once appeared relatively safe for Republicans are increasingly becoming battlegrounds—potentially giving Democrats more opportunities to make gains in November. Meanwhile, Cook has shifted Michigan’s 8th Congressional District from “Lean Democrat” to “Likely Democrat” following Republican primary turmoil. Trump-endorsed candidate Amir Hassan unexpectedly lost the August 4 primary to Tom Smith, who had previously dropped out of the race, leaving Smith with less than three months to build a campaign against incumbent Democratic Representative Kristen McDonald Rivet. McDonald Rivet won the district by 7 points in 2024, even as Trump carried it by 2, Cook notes, and she enters the general election with a significant war chest advantage. Map Shows Shift in 3 Congressional Races Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins.
news.summary: The shifts in the races are notable because both Florida and Michigan backed Trump statewide in 2024.

news.title: ‘True American icon’: Politicians pay tribute to Dolly Parton
news.text:
Politicians were among the figures leading tributes to Dolly Parton following her death, with Donald Trump, Barack Obama and Kamala Harris among those honoring the country music legend.

Donald Trump announced that American flags across the United States would be lowered for one week to honor Parton following her death.

Trump paid tribute to Parton on Truth Social, describing her as one of the “greatest Country singers” and calling her passing “a true loss for millions.”

Barack Obama honored Parton on X, highlighting her 11 Grammy Awards, extensive philanthropy and support for research that led to the Moderna COVID vaccine.

Kamala Harris remembered Parton as “a true American icon,” praising her music, kindness and the distribution of more than 300 million books through her Imagination Library.

news.title: Democratic Voters Reject Resistance Stars
news.text:
There has been a lot of commentary on the differences between Resistance 1.0, the effort by anti-Trump activists to bring down President Donald Trump in his first term, and Resistance 2.0, the effort by anti-Trump activists to bring down Trump in his second term. There are some tactical contrasts, but the simple fact is, they're still at it.

This year's election season has featured two much-lauded figures of Resistance 1.0 as they tried to use their anti-Trump agitation as a springboard to public office. Alex Vindman, the former National Security Council staffer who in 2019 set off the first Trump impeachment, ran for U.S. Senate in Florida, and George Conway, the lawyer who talked E. Jean Carroll into suing Trump, ran for the House in New York.

Both suffered crushing defeats in Democrat primaries.

Conway ran in New York's 12th Congressional District, in Manhattan, the seat vacated by the retirement of Democratic Rep. Jerry Nadler. There were a lot of candidates. Conway finished fifth, with 6.1 percent of the vote. A wealthy lawyer, Conway loaned his campaign $2 million for the run. In all, he spent $5.7 million.

The money allowed Conway to mount a vanity campaign, to publicly fantasize about getting Trump, and to pound his chest about the massive damage judgment against Trump in the Carroll trial. "Hi, Donald! It's me, George Conway," began one ad. "I cost you $88 million fking dollars, and I've only just gotten started." For his next act, Conway promised to put Trump in jail.

Conway obviously thought the theme might work in New York's 12th, in which Kamala Harris beat Trump 81 percent to 17 percent in the 2024 presidential election. But of course all Democrats in the race promised to oppose Trump. The Democrat voters' job was to choose the best. Conway was not their first, second, third or fourth choice. Instead, the primary winner was a member of the New York state assembly named Micah C. Lasher, who pledged to stand up to Trump.

The other Resistance star to face-plant was Vindman, who in 2019, as an active-duty Army lieutenant colonel on the staff of the National Security Council, set in motion the first impeachment of Trump. Vindman, who was privy to some of the president's calls with world leaders, felt that Trump had committed some sort of unspecified violation in a conversation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Vindman relayed secret information to a friend in the CIA, who came up with a "whistleblower" complaint against the president.

The impeachment failed, of course. Under pressure from the Trump administration, Vindman retired from the military and began trading on his notoriety. He wrote a memoir called "Here, Right Matters," with the title based on his congressional testimony. He started a company called Here Right Matters LLC. It did well; in a financial disclosure form this year, Vindman listed around $1.5 million in income from that and other ventures. The Alexander Vindman business did pretty well.

The next step would be politics. Vindman moved to Florida and ran for the Senate as a Democrat. When he jumped into the race in January, his announcement video began with news clips from his role in the Trump impeachment. A moment later, Vindman said, as pictures of his congressional testimony played: "The last time you saw me was here, swearing an oath to tell the truth about a president who broke his. See, my family came to America as refugees to escape tyranny. And I sure as hell was not going to bow down to some wannabe tyrant. This president unleashed a reign of terror and retribution, not just against me and my family, but against all of us."

No subtlety there; the Hero of the Resistance had arrived to take on Trump! Vindman raised $16 million for his campaign, while his Democratic socialist opponent, Angie Nixon, raised a little less than $1 million. Vindman immediately became a heavy favorite to win the Democrat nomination. He remained the favorite until Election Day, when Nixon shocked the political world by trouncing Vindman, 56 percent to 44 percent.

Once again, the Resistance 1.0 magic did not work. As it had been in Manhattan, only on a far larger scale, Florida Democrat voters just didn't care that a candidate had led one of the many unsuccessful efforts to drive Trump out of office from 2017 to 2021. That doesn't mean they like or support Trump; they absolutely don't. But it does mean that all the excitement that Conway and Vindman and their allies stirred up in the wayback time of Trump 1.0 truly came to nothing.

A longtime progressive operative, a veteran of past Democratic campaigns, agreed with that sentiment.

“Trying to cancel folks on the Left for their associations with someone who doesn’t agree with you politically — I just don’t think that’s an effective tactic,” that person explained. “It’s grasping for straws.”

The operative argued that Piker’s inflammatory style is itself part of what attracts younger voters who have grown distrustful of conventional political messaging.

“They don’t think he’s full of s***,” the operative said. “He’s not only speaking for himself, but he’s speaking for a kind of silent majority in a way and on issues that — they’re used to hearing lines from politicians that they know are full of s***, and I think it’s refreshing.”

A former senior Biden administration official pointed to another element of Piker’s appeal: his ability to project a cultural image far removed from the stereotype Republicans have sought to attach to Democratic men in the Trump era.

“I think this is something we’ve talked about in the past,” the official said. “Hasan works out all the time. He’s good-looking. He presents himself as an ‘alpha.’ It sounds stupid, but this stuff actually does matter, especially when engaging with voters who aren’t locked in on politics the same way you and I are.”

“I mean this with all due respect,” the official added. “Who do you think regular guys relate to more? The Pod Save America crew, or some gym bro streaming from his bedroom while packing Zyns?”

That view is far from universal within the Democratic Party.

Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-MA), who had already disavowed Piker, stated during a weekend appearance on Fox News Sunday that “the Democratic Party does not stand for what Hasan Piker stands for.”

Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-MI) went further on Monday, calling Piker “a hack who thrives on hate, shock and awe because he lacks substance.”

“Hasan Piker’s talk of violence against American Jews, and directly naming a Michigan elected official, and future member of Congress, Jeremy Moss, is unacceptable. Full stop,” she said in a statement. “We should all be calling out this disgusting rhetoric so it loses its grip on our politics once and for all. It has no place in Michigan, and no place in our country.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) on Tuesday joined the condemnation, saying that Piker’s comments regarding Jewish Americans were “malicious” and “should not be tolerated by anyone in the public square.”

“There is zero justification for threats against the safety of our Jewish brothers and sisters at a moment of rising hate. We will fight the cancer of antisemitism with the fierce urgency of now,” he added.

Yet Peter Loge, a professor at George Washington University’s School of Media and Public Affairs, questioned whether the Piker controversies will ultimately matter when voters go to the polls.

Loge said voters tend to be driven by issues much closer to home, arguing that despite narratives about the effect of the war in Gaza on the 2024 presidential election, the surveys he has reviewed suggest inflation played a far greater role in former Vice President Kamala Harris’s defeat.

Ultimately, Loge stated that popular pundits making inflammatory comments is not the sole province of Democrats.

“Hasan Piker is obviously very popular, and part of the reason he’s popular is because he says what he thinks. There’s also a bit of outrage, and you know being measured doesn’t get clicks, and so you want to be a bit outrageous. I think that’s a challenge that both Democrats and Republicans face,” Loge explained. “Republicans occasionally have to distance themselves from Tucker Carlson or someone like that. I think that the best answer to all of this might actually be, if I were advising one of these candidates and asked about Piker, I would say, ‘Look, what matters is people are really angry, and he’s really poking hard at stuff that a lot of people think are important.'”

news.title: Police From GOP-leaning Counties Set To Fight Against New York ICE Law
news.text: A new law banning police and sheriff's departments in New York from working with federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) took effect Tuesday, facing immediate pushback from areas of the state that voted for President Donald Trump in 2024. The law—the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act—was signed by Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul in May. It prohibits local governments and law enforcement agencies from entering into, renewing, extending or remaining in so-called 287(g) agreements with ICE. Most of the localities that entered into those agreements are in areas that backed Trump's White House bid. "Any police department or sheriff's office that disobeys this law that maintains any agreement with ICE will face legal action," Hochul said at a press conference on Tuesday. The law has drawn praise from immigrant-rights advocates and sharp criticism from some county leaders and sheriffs, several of whom have argued that such agreements with federal agencies can help identify criminals in local custody and improve cooperation. Multiple agencies that have complied with the ban have come together to fight the new law in court. "Although I must comply with this law while it remains in effect, I will not remain silent about its hypocrisy or its consequences," Cattaraugus County Sheriff Eric Butler told Newsweek. "Today, I am joining 21 other New York sheriffs in filing suit against Governor Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James to challenge the State’s action. "Compliance is not agreement, and it is not surrender," Butler said. What Is a 287(g) Agreement? The federal 287(g) program allows ICE to delegate certain immigration enforcement powers to state and local law enforcement agencies through formal agreements. The program was created under the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996. Under ICE's current framework, agreements generally fall into three categories: Supporters of the program argue that it helps remove people who pose public-safety threats. Opponents and critics say that the agreements divert local resources toward federal civil immigration enforcement and can undermine trust between immigrant communities and local police. In Trump's second stint in the Oval Office, the number of agencies joining the program has soared, particularly in Republican-leaning areas. Because local police and sheriff's departments have not worked with the federal government, DHS said over 6,900 known illegal immigrants with criminal records or charges had been released rather than handed over to federal agents between January 20, 2025, and December 1, 2025. “Governor Hochul must stop putting politics above public safety. This type of insanity leads to more crimes and more innocent victims," a DHS spokesperson told Newsweek on Tuesday. Hochul said Tuesday that the 287(g) ban would not affect whether criminals were turned over to ICE, telling reporters that police would assist federal agents "only if a real crime has been committed. But on civil immigration matters, ICE is on their own." Which New York Agencies Were Participating? Records reviewed by Newsweek show that county sheriff's offices and police departments in several parts of New York had entered into 287(g) agreements before the state ban took effect. The New York Attorney General's office identified 12 agencies as having agreements affected by the law, while ICE records show active agreements in eight instances across five counties as recently as August 2026. Newsweek contacted affected law enforcement agencies for comment Tuesday morning. Among the agencies identified were: ICE records indicate Nassau, Niagara, Steuben, Cattaraugus and Rensselaer had agreements including task-force, warrant-service and jail-enforcement arrangements. Butler said that the new state law would not stop his department or others from cooperating with ICE, including locating known individuals with valid criminal arrest warrants. Steuben County Sheriff James Allard told Newsweek that the change would mean departments would not be reimbursed by DHS for protecting federal agents and citizens, adding, "It is a political platform during a reelection year and does nothing to keep our citizens safer." Otsego County Sheriff Richard J. Devlin Jr. was also defiant in his message, telling Newsweek, "My oath is to the people of this county—not to politics or an agenda. I will enforce the law, protect our communities, and always put public safety first." Many Participating Counties Lean Republican Many of these counties favored Trump in the 2024 election, some of them heavily. Trump carried Cattaraugus County with roughly 66 percent of the vote, Steuben County with nearly 66 percent, Niagara County with about 57 percent and Nassau County with just over 51 percent. Rensselaer County was the exception among some of the highest-profile jurisdictions, narrowly backing then-Vice President Kamala Harris, but the county's leaders have taken a strong stance against Hochul's ban. “We have yet to hear the Governor or Attorney General tell us how their action makes our state or Rensselaer County any safer. We are still waiting for an answer to that important question," Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault said in a statement shared to Facebook Monday. “As Sheriff, I am party to this legal action and submitted an affidavit in support. I believe that when the facts of this case are heard and the political arguments are set aside, we will prevail." What Happens Next? The key question now is whether courts will allow the move to stand. Rensselaer County officials have already announced plans to challenge the law and argue that cooperation agreements with ICE help local authorities identify dangerous offenders and improve public safety. Hochul and Democratic Attorney General Letitia James have countered that local police resources should remain focused on local crimes rather than federal civil immigration enforcement. "No county executive should think that they are above the law in the state of New York," Hochul said Tuesday. The legal dispute could offer a significant test of how far states can go in restricting local participation in federal immigration initiatives. While the federal government cannot generally compel states to carry out immigration enforcement duties, states often have broad authority to regulate the conduct of their own agencies and political subdivisions. If the law survives judicial scrutiny, New York will become one of the most prominent examples of a state explicitly prohibiting local participation in the 287(g) program. If the counties prevail, some agencies could seek to restore agreements with ICE and resume participation in federal immigration enforcement programs. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Geoffrey Rowland.
news.summary: Governor Kathy Hochul said any police or sheriff departments still working with DHS could face legal action.

news.title: Dolly Parton’s Views on Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton, Explained
news.text:
Dolly Parton built one of the most beloved careers in country music while carefully keeping distance from the political worlds of Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton.

Parton, the iconic country music star widely celebrated as one of the genre’s defining voices, died Tuesday at 80, leaving behind an extraordinary catalog of songs and a devoted global fan base in mourning.

Even with her enormous cultural reach, Parton long resisted being pulled into partisan battles, often choosing to keep her views on the country’s most divisive issues private.

During the 2016 presidential race, she made clear that she had not endorsed either Trump or Clinton after comments praising the Democratic nominee’s qualifications were widely interpreted as political support.

That cautious approach continued in 2020, when she declined to publicly back either Joe Biden or Trump, and again in 2024, when she avoided taking sides in the contest between Kamala Harris and the Republican.

In a 2023 interview, Parton summed up her reluctance to wade into politics with characteristic bluntness: ‘Because you’re going to lose half your audience.’

She also acknowledged that the sharp political divide between Trump and Biden had seeped into everyday life, making even family gatherings tense. ‘Especially if people are drinking – they get in a damn fight at the table,’ she told The Guardian.

Trump offered Parton the Presidential Medal of Freedom twice during his first administration, but she turned it down both times, first citing her husband’s illness and later concerns over COVID and travel.

When Biden was considering giving her the medal, Parton said she wasn’t sure she’d accept because taking it could look political. She ultimately declined it as well.

The last time Parton appeared comfortable stepping foot inside the political realm was back in 2005 when George W. Bush presented her with the National Medal of the Arts.

She was hosted at the White House the following year by Bush and First Lady Laura Bush as a Kennedy Center honoree. 

Parton explained that she ‘hated politics’ because it forced people to pick sides.

‘I’ve got as many Democrats as I do Republicans as fans, and I’m not going to insult any of them because I care about all of them,’ she said in 2023.

‘I ain’t that good a Christian to think that I am so good that I can judge people. That’s God’s job, not mine. So as far as politics, I hate politics. Hate politics.’

But she said that just because she chose to stay out of politics didn’t mean she didn’t have strong opinions on the issues of the day. 

When pressed about Trump during an appearance on ABC’s Nightline in 2018, she said: ‘Of course I have my opinion about everybody and everything. But I learned a long time ago, keep your damn mouth shut if you want to stay in show business.’

‘I’m not in politics, I’m an entertainer,’ she added.

But Parton’s refusal to come down on one side of the political aisle didn’t mean she was indifferent to the world.

She released World on Fire three years ago, a song that attacked politicians without naming a party.

‘Don’t get me started on politics,’ she sang. ‘Greedy politicians, present and past, they wouldn’t know the truth if it bit ’em in the ass.’ 

Parton said that the lyrics had been provoked because was was ‘fearful’ about the world.

Watching the world just burn down around us with all the craziness, all the war, all the famine and the politics – you know, the great divide, I guess, is more what I’m talking about – and what it’s even doing to families, even my own,’ she told NPR after the song’s release.

news.title: Trump Breaks Silence Amid Dolly Parton Death Rumors Spreading
news.text:
Donald Trump honored Dolly Parton after her death at 80, directing that American flags be flown at half-staff across the country for a full week in tribute to the music icon.

‘Very sad to report that Dolly Parton, one of the greatest Country singers, and far beyond, EVER, has just passed away,’ the president wrote in a post on Truth Social.

Trump described Parton’s passing as a devastating loss felt by millions of admirers and said the flag order would take effect Tuesday evening.

‘There has never been anyone like her, and never will,’ Trump added. ‘Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you.’

Parton, widely celebrated as the queen of country music, leaves behind an extraordinary catalog of songs, a cultural legacy that stretched far beyond Nashville and generations of fans now mourning her loss.

Trump had frequently spoken warmly of Parton over the years, and during his first administration she was twice offered the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

She declined the initial offer because her husband, Carl Dean, was unwell, and later passed on the second opportunity because she did not want to travel during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Despite her enormous public profile, Parton long kept her political beliefs private, steering clear of partisan debate even as political divisions in the United States grew sharper.

Parton’s home-state senators also paid tribute, with Marsha Blackburn saying there were ‘no words to adequately express the sorrow’ felt by her family and Tennesseans and declaring: ‘Dolly, we will always love you.’

Bill Hagerty said he and his wife, Chrissy, were ‘deeply saddened’ by the loss of a ‘dear friend’ and ‘entrepreneurial juggernaut’ who helped transform Tennessee while bringing joy to millions through her music and philanthropy.

The legendary country singer’s death was confirmed today in an Instagram video posted by her nephew Bryan Seaver, who also served as her head of security.

‘This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago before I fully absorbed it as a future reality,’ Seaver revealed.

Her passing came after months of health woes that saw her pull out of a string of public appearances, fueling fan fears for her wellbeing.

Parton’s determination to remain above partisan politics continued throughout Trump’s rise despite pressure from media critics to declare where she stood.

She clarified in 2016 that she had endorsed neither Trump nor Hillary Clinton after her praise of Clinton’s qualifications was mistaken for an endorsement.

Parton again refused to take sides during the 2020 election and stayed out of Trump’s race against Kamala Harris four years later.

Parton generally avoided White House events and kept her distance from sitting politicians, regardless of party.

Her last known public appearance with a sitting president came in December 2006, when George W. Bush welcomed her to the White House before she was celebrated at the Kennedy Center Honors. 

Parton, however, was openly enthusiastic about Barack Obama early in his presidency, telling Larry King in 2009 that he was ‘going to be a great president’ and urging Americans to ‘get behind him, pray for him, support him, and hope for the best.’

By JACK TOLEDO

Published: 18:37 BST, 25 August 2026 | Updated: 18:37 BST, 25 August 2026

Gavin Newsom listed his gorgeous $7.5 million home for sale in California as speculation grows that he may run for president in 2028.

The governor of California, 58, listed the more than 12,000sq ft residence in Fair Oaks on Monday as he is widely viewed as a leading contender for the Democratic presidential nomination.

Newsom has built a national political profile through his battles with Trump, his fundraising network and his aggressive social media presence - all of which have fueled speculation about his ambitions.

His stunning property features amenities similar to a world-class resort, including a full-size tennis court, 5,000-bottle wine cellar, a private pool, cold plunge and hot tub.

Newsom broke the record for the highest sale ever in Fair Oaks when he bought the home for $3.7 million and could break that record again if the house is purchased for his asking price.

The listing of the seven-bedroom, 12-bathroom house comes just four months before Newsom's term as governor comes to an end.

'With the governor's term ending in January 2027, the family began a gradual transition in 2024, purchasing a home in Marin County to provide continuity for their children's education,' Newsom spokesperson Izzy Gardon said in a statement.

'The sale of their Sacramento home is the next step in that transition.'

Gavin Newsom, 58, listed the more than 12,000sq ft residence in Fair Oaks, California on Monday for $7.5million

The more than 12,000sq ft residence features amenities similar to a world-class resort, including a full-size tennis court, 5,000-bottle wine cellar, a private pool, cold plunge and hot tub

Splitting time between two properties was likely not fitting the common-man persona Newsom has recently put on. 

He is now relocating to a humbler six-bedroom mansion in Kentfield, just outside of San Francisco, which he purchased in 2024 for $9.1 million.

Users on Facebook ripped the governor apart for his elite lifestyle and questioned how he could afford such properties.

'Wait what was that thing about No Kings? Looks like a palace to me… hmmm,' wrote one user. 

'Wow, it pays a lot to be the Governor of California,' another added.

'So, the Governor owns a $7.5million dollar home and a $9million dollar home,' a third said. 'Tell me where the train money, homeless and diaper money went?'

Aside from Newsom's move to a new mansion, several prominent figures have criticized the governor for attempting to downplay his lavish lifestyle, portraying himself as more relatable to potential voters ahead of a possible 2028 presidential run.

Users on Facebook criticized the governor's elite lifestyle 

Another questioned how Newsom was able to afford his properties on a governor's salary 

A third appeared take issue with Newsom's way of living as well 

Despite the jockeying among potential candidates, former Vice President Kamala Harris remains the leading Democrat in a June RealClear Polling poll, with Newsom and Pete Buttigieg also among names receiving significant attention.

According to the RealClear Polling figures, Harris was at 27.1 percent, followed by Newsom at 17.49 percent, Buttigieg at 13 percent and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at 11.9 percent.

Those numbers are only an early snapshot of a contest that is still far from taking shape.

Joe Rogan, a former California resident and longtime critic of Newsom, labeled him a 'con man.'

'Nobody wants President Newsom either. Nobody believes in that guy. That guy's a f**king con man,' Rogan said at the time.

'I mean, everything he did in California, from trying to mandate vaccines for kids when it was totally unnecessary to being caught out in public without a mask and lying about the fact that he was outdoors. All of it.

Podcaster Joe Rogan, a long-time critic of Newsom, previously has called the governor a 'con man'. Newsom came under fire presenting a common man persona 

'It's just, nobody believes in the guy. He's just a politician, just a stone-cold, narrative-driven politician, you know, and nobody thinks he's a real human.'

Newsom also came under intense scrutiny in February after he attended an event in Atlanta, Georgia, to promote his memoir, Young Man in a Hurry.

The governor was asked about his lifelong struggle with dyslexia, to which he responded: 'I'm not trying to impress you. I'm just trying to impress upon you. I'm like you. I'm no better than you.'

'You know, I'm a 960 SAT guy... you've never seen me read a speech because I cannot read a speech,' he said to a predominantly black crowd.

Rapper Nicki Minaj, an outspoken supporter of Donald Trump, responded to the clip by claiming Newsom was trying to appeal to black voters by telling 'them how stupid he is & that he can't read.'

Minaj then accused the governor of slowing down his speech by talking in a 'sporadic cadence.'

'He's not just TELLING them that they're all probably stupid & probably can't read, he's LITERALLY SLOW-ING-DOWN-HIS-SPEECH to make them understand the words that are coming out of his mouth!!!! As if they're children!!!!' 

Rapper Nicki Minaj accused Newsom of trying to appeal to black voters by claiming he does not know how to read after he attended an event in Atlanta, Georgia, to promote his memoir in February 

Newsom's spokesperson responded to the right-wing outrage by telling the Daily Mail: 'First MAGA mocked his dyslexia and now they're calling him racist for talking about his low SAT scores. This is fake MAGA-manufactured outrage.'

'The Governor has said this publicly for years, including with Charlie Kirk and dozens of other audiences. The same people who excused or ignored Trump's racist ape video can go f**k themselves.'

Rogan and Vice President JD Vance shared a laugh together in July at Newsom's expense as they also discussed Newsom's words at the event in Atlanta.

The podcaster and vice president agreed that Newsom was 'full of s**t.'

'Admirably full of s**t,' said Rogan. 'I admire the sheer tenacity that he has in being full of st. It really is amazing.'

Newsom called Rogan obsessed earlier this month and labeled him an 'a**hole.'

That's just not true. We have more illegals because Democrats like Joe Biden and Kamala Harris let them into the country almost entirely unchecked.

news.title: No, the Democratic Party is not shifting on Israel
news.text:
Recent progressive wins of outspoken Israel critics in Democratic primaries have generated a lot of optimism. Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic nomination for a Senate seat in Michigan after AIPAC and its allies spent more than $54m against him in what came to be the most expensive Democratic Senate primary in US history.

In New Jersey, a surgeon named Adam Hamawy, who as a medical volunteer refused to leave Gaza until the last member of his team could evacuate, won a 12-person primary in a House of Representatives race.

Years ago, such breakthroughs would have seemed impossible. For many on the left, it now seems like their hard work at the grassroots level is paying off.

And yet, all the talk of a “shift on Israel” within the Democratic Party is premature. The Democratic establishment remains firmly in the Israeli camp, even if it is striking a more critical tone ahead of the midterm elections. We should not mistake election-season displays of sympathy for a human-rights awakening on Palestine.

We have now reached a point where the shift in attitudes towards Israel can no longer be ignored. A May poll by New York Times/Siena suggested that nearly three-quarters of Democratic voters did not approve of aid for Israel. Another survey by Quinnipiac University showed that 66 percent of Democrats thought the US was too supportive of Israel. These numbers have made the Democratic leadership realise that open support for genocidaires is becoming too costly politically. Democratic voters, who watched a livestreamed genocide, clearly no longer see Palestine as a secondary issue in their political and moral choices.

This awareness has finally come after Democratic leaders spent 2024 attacking students who protested the genocide on campuses across the country. Prominent Democratic members of Congress called the protest encampment at Columbia University a gathering of “anti-Israel, anti-Jewish activists” and a “breeding ground” for anti-Semitic attacks and demanded that the university dismantle it. Many praised the violent crackdowns on the student protesters.

Former State Department Spokesperson Matthew Miller now admits Israel “without a doubt” committed war crimes.

But enough Democratic Representatives still voted with the Republican majority against it. The vote was politically useful precisely because it was powerless. The 103 Democratic votes in favour of cutting aid to Israel gave the party something to campaign on, while ensuring Israel still had the weapons it needs to continue its brutality.

It is a strategy that the party is likely to repeat in the next Congress to secure Israeli interests while appearing to acknowledge voters’ demands.

Furthermore, the Democratic establishment has shown little interest in breaking its dependence on AIPAC. In April, the Democratic National Committee rejected even a symbolic resolution condemning the lobby’s interference in Democratic primaries.

AIPAC, meanwhile, has responded to its growing toxicity by learning how to disappear. Its super PAC has routed millions through other organisations whose funding is disclosed only after voters cast their ballots. It has also directed donors through candidate-specific portals that leave individual names, rather than AIPAC’s, in public campaign records.

Having spent more than $100m on this midterm race, AIPAC will continue to influence Democratic congressional politics to ensure it is in favour of the Israeli government.

Its defeat in a number of Democratic primaries is significant, but we should remember the limits of that. We have to recognise that the elected progressives, while critical of Israel, are not prepared to go all the way on recognising Palestinian rights.

Representative Ro Khanna, for example, has been calling for aid cuts to Israel and an end to financing for the Iron Dome. He even went on a visit to the occupied West Bank where he witnessed settler violence firsthand.

Brad Lander, who won the New York primary for a House seat in June and was backed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, has described what is happening in Gaza as genocide. And yet, his criticism goes only that far. He identifies as a “liberal Zionist” and has made clear he does not support BDS.

That is true. And yet, achieving a true shift in the Democratic Party can go a long way in helping us in our pursuit of freedom.

That is why we should support every progressive candidate willing to confront AIPAC and Israel in November, because every seat won places another potential vote for Palestinian human rights inside a Congress that has spent decades denying them.

Movements build power by turning each election into leverage for the next fight and continuing the pressure on elected officials even after they take office. We must reject every attempt by the Democratic Party to pay lip service to our cause; we must continue to push for real action on Israel.

news.title: INGERSOLL: Well Well Well, If It Isn’t Consequences
news.text:
Below is State of the Day, a morning newsletter by Daily Caller Editor-at-Large Geoff Ingersoll. Sign up here.

Greetings, Dear Reader,

I was reading the Bible last night. St. Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter six, verses 1-5 and verses 7-8.

My friends, if anyone is detected in a transgression, you who have received the Spirit should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness. Take care that you yourselves are not tempted. 2 Bear one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ. 3 For if those who are nothing think they are something, they deceive themselves. 4 All must test their own work; then that work, rather than their neighbor’s work, will become a cause for pride. 5 For all must carry their own loads.

7 Do not be deceived; God is not mocked, for you reap whatever you sow. 8 If you sow to your own flesh, you will reap corruption from the flesh; but if you sow to the Spirit, you will reap eternal life from the Spirit.

WELL WELL WELL, IF IT ISN’T CONSEQUENCES

One of the most fundamental planks of Western civilization is that individual liberty is tied directly to responsibility. The man who takes on responsibility and delivers on that responsibility is afforded more liberty than the man who does not.

It seems counterintuitive, but it’s true. If you take care of your family, take care in your work, and take care of your community, then that community will afford you more options or opportunities than you had starting off.

Do deadbeat, drug addict criminals get small business loans? Probably not. Does the guy with six local car dealerships who sponsors the little league team and attends church routinely? Probably so.

While Paul encourages charity and community – “if anyone is detected in a transgression, you … should restore such a one in the spirit of gentleness” and “bear one another’s burdens” – he’s clear on ultimate responsibility – “all must carry their own loads,” and most famously, “you reap whatever you sow.”

All of this, however, assumes the community itself is healthy.

I don’t think it’s the least bit exaggerated to say one political party in this country does just about everything it can to encourage avoidance of responsibility.

It’s generally the party of “root causes.” Oddly enough, treating these so-called “causes” almost never works. In June 2021, Kamala Harris famously traveled down to South America to treat the “root causes” of illegal immigration. A record 10 million illegal crossings occurred in the three years after that.

Nice work, K-Rock!

And that’s the Democrat establishment. Let’s check on their left flank.

DSA National Political Committee member Frances Gill sat down with Conan Nolan of NBC4 Los Angeles.

Frances Gill: What we really want to see is a horizon where folks are not reliant on armed enforcement to meet our public safety needs.

Nolan: Right, but it says “defund police” on your website — that’s your goal — and also to get rid of prisons and jails, correct?

Gill: Correct. / Yes.

Nolan: So if my daughter is assaulted and raped, is there any agency that would seek to find her assailant and bring him to justice?

Gill: Of course, yeah of course—

Nolan: What would it be if not police and where would he be if not a jail?

Gill: So I guess I really want to avoid getting caught into these hypotheticals and talk more about the reality that we’re actually facing right now, which is that we’re spending absolutely outrageous amounts of money on police and policing. And we’re not spending money on things that actually make people safe and feel safe, which is things like actually well-lit streets.

Things like mental health care and substance use treatment … so things that drive people to commit crimes and to make our society less safe. We’re not doing anything about the root causes and instead we’re funneling the money into the police.

Sure, Frances, it’s broken street lights “driving” criminals to commit crimes.

This is not just a position of DSA members and campus radicals with septum piercings. It’s the whole enchilada, from militant socialists to old Joe Biden himself.

The prestigious New England Journal of Medicine just published a piece arguing in all seriousness that Jason Arday (RIP) of Cambridge did nothing wrong except be black in academia. In fact, everyone is cheating in academia, the piece argues.

Instead of perhaps holding Arday accountable first, then the rapidly hollowing rigors of academia, who does the author blame? Racism, of course. You probably don’t have to guess, but that’s a “root cause” of Arday’s outcome in this case.

From the elite to the indebted barista with advanced degrees, from the establishment to the truly radical, virtually nobody on the political left wants a system where individual men are held accountable for their actions.

Right now, I’m supposed to be upset about Yasmany Moreno de Armas, a Cuban national who was deported to the Central African Republic. He crossed into the US illegally by raft in 2016. Nine years later, in 2025, he was detained and deportation proceedings kicked off.

Was it my personal responsibility to make sure de Armas spent his (illegal) nine years in the US wisely? That he coached himself up enough on Cuban relations with the US to know he could not be deported back to Cuba? That he seriously considered taking the ~$3,000 pay out and self deporting?

Now he’s in the Congo and CBS is bellyaching about his outcome. Nobody on the left in this debate can muster the courage to discuss how de Armas’s choices led to his being in the Congo.

In worst case scenarios, the left’s anathema for holding people accountable results in others bearing the burden.

Trump’s DHS just picked up an illegal in one of the wealthiest counties in America for selling fentanyl outside a public school. He was caught in 2016 under Obama and released into the country. In 2024, the Biden DHS encountered him and let him go.

“The Loudon County Sheriff says investigators ID’d him as a dealer connected to overdoses of students at Park View High School in May 2026,” Fox’s Bill Melugin reported Monday.

Students OD’d. What were the “root causes” of those students ODing? Was it not enough guidance counselors in the school? Not enough resources in the richest county in Virginia?

The root cause in this case was Democrat policies of leniency.

They actually hate real love.

They do too.

Newsom is another almost-certain 2028 contender who has sought to appeal to socialists. During remarks on July 9 at an elementary school in Davis, Newsom said he would gladly campaign for socialists and progressives, including Randy Villegas, to help Democrats retake power in Congress. During a previous appearance with Jack Cocchiarella on a livestream on his YouTube channel in early July, Newsom argued that including socialists is part of the idea of having a “big tent party,” an essential to taking back majorities in the House and Senate this fall.

“Look, I’m for addition, not subtraction,” the California governor said. “The Democratic Party needs to be in the addition business if we’re going to get back into the majority. Yeah, we need to get our base out there. We got to turn out. … I’m not offended by this notion of a big tent.”

“And I know the purity tests are going to get tougher and tougher in the next few years. But I am enthusiastic about the success and the energy and the vibrancy that’s happening at the grassroots in this country. I think it’s a healthy damn thing,” he added. 

DEMOCRATS FROM OPPOSITE SIDES OF PARTY ALL RALLY BEHIND ‘BIG TENT’

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez

Ocasio-Cortez, who fueled the rise of socialism in New York and consequently nationwide, with her support for Mayor Zohran Mamdani, has similarly continued to align herself with elements of the movement, including by endorsing DSA members David Orkin, Christian Celeste Tate, and Eon Huntley in May. The New York Democrat has declined to distance herself from other socialist candidates who have stoked controversy, including DSA members State Assemblywomen Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier.

“These are two young, talented, intelligent women that got elected against all odds — against millions of dollars. Although the DSA has not held a favorable view of former Vice President Kamala Harris in the past, she appears to be courting socialist support this year ahead of a second possible presidential bid. Aside from the top tier of likely Democratic contenders, several more possible mainstream candidates are holding off on embracing socialists while still offering olive branches to the movement. Those include Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA), who endorsed el Sayed and has been described by Piker as his “dark-horse pick” for 2028.

“I don’t spend much time thinking about factional, Democratic politics,” Ossoff told CNN in June, adding that the divide “exists more in those places and for those people and groups for whom the Democratic primary is the horizon of politics.”

news.text:
Dubbed the "Nostradamus" of predicting presidential election results by using his famous “Keys to the White House,” historian Allan Lichtman will debut a different set of keys focused on evaluating presidential greatness in a new book coming out next month.

“Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation” will be on shelves Sept. 22, and the distinguished history professor at American University is already working on the natural follow-up book — “Worst American Presidents.”

 He says that will certainly feature the current president.

“Donald Trump will definitively be making an appearance in my worst presidents book, along with a rogues gallery of presidents like James Buchanan, Andrew Johnson, Herbert Hoover,” Lichtman told Raw Story.

In “Great American Presidents,” Lichtman includes a preliminary ranking of modern presidents since Ronald Reagan, putting Trump at the very bottom. 

“We have never seen a president who so fundamentally threatens American democracy. He has openly said, ‘As president, I can do anything I want.’ Not surprisingly, he cozies up to the dictators of the world,” Lichtman said.

“He seems to be bringing this dictatorial, authoritarian approach to American politics. We've also seen the fact that he bases his presidency on blatant lies ... Not to mention the fact that his policies have been an abject disaster."

Lichtman presents in the book 10 keys to presidential greatness, focused on “the consequences of the president, not necessarily whether you agree with everything they've done.” Types of keys range from how presidents handled crises to their moral vision and narrative abilities.

 Allan Lichtman (Photo Credit: Sam Lichtman, used with permission)

Franklin D. Roosevelt tops Lichtman’s list, followed by Abraham Lincoln. 

Lyndon B. Johnson might surprise some with the third highest ranking, but Lichtman argues Johnson’s “extraordinary depth and breadth of domestic accomplishment … merits the designation as a great president, despite the tragedy of Vietnam.”

That legacy includes the development of the Voting Rights Act, the Civil Rights Act and Medicare and Medicaid programs during his presidency. 

Another surprise among great American presidents might be the lesser known James K. Polk, Lichtman said, who ranked him 11th in the top 12.

“Although a one-term president, a racist, an imperialist, James K. Polk transformed the nation,” Lichtman said.

“He basically doubled the size of the continental United States.

While Lichtman’s book looks at more than 200 years of American presidents, he argues this type of book is needed today “to show that we can achieve great leadership,” particularly as polled Americans overwhelmingly express disapproval with the direction of the country. 

On Monday, Trump’s approval rating hit its lowest point at 33 percent, according to new Reuters/Ipsos polling.

“We can put into place presidents who transform and redeem the nation,” Lichtman said. “'Great American Presidents’ is, I think, the needed antidote to the despair that so many Americans seem to be showing right now. It shows what our nation can become.”

Lichtman’s keys indicate that the U.S. has lacked a great president since Reagan due to “the increasing complexity and difficulty of the office, the increasing polarization of our politics.”

The midterms will be “pivotal” as the policy achievements of some of Lichtman’s greatest presidents are at stake under Trump's leadership, he said.

“This is the biggest backlash against voting rights that we've seen since the end of Reconstruction and the adoption of Jim Crow in the South,” Lichtman said. 

“We're also seeing the undermining of other great initiatives of Lyndon Johnson. For example, the so-called Big Beautiful Bill — I call it the Big Ugly Bill — gives huge tax breaks to big corporations and the rich.” 

Lichtman agrees with the prediction of a much-discussed blue wave in the November elections, giving Democrats control of the House again. Senate control shifting to Democrats seems to be about a “50-50” chance, and the "gerrymandering war that Trump started" might backfire, Lichtman said.

“Are we going to redeem the domestic legacy of Franklin Roosevelt, Johnson, or are we going to move into a new era in which public policy favors the wealthy and undermines support for the more marginal and less affluent peoples in this country?”

However, the blue wave in the midterms relies on the elections being “free and fair,” which is of particular concern to Lichtman as Trump continues to push lies about election fraud since 2020.

“When Trump talks about election integrity, that's just code word for his interfering in elections,” Lichtman said. 

The Justice Department announced on Tuesday last week plans to deploy 1,000 federal monitors to polling places for the midterms.

“In my view, it is a direct attempt at election interference and rigging,” Lichtman said.

‘Come out of the darkness’

“Great American Presidents” attempts to “codify historical judgment” in a similar way to how Lichtman’s “Keys to the White House” applied mathematical models used to predict earthquakes to election prediction.

“Like the ‘Keys to the White House,’ which were the world's only do-it-yourself presidential prediction system, the ‘10 Keys’ enables anyone to be a do-it-yourself evaluator of presidents,” Lichtman said.

 Book cover (Credit: Christine Van Bree Design)

Lichtman had a near-perfect presidential election prediction record for more than 40 years using the model until Kamala Harris lost the 2024 presidential election.

Unprecedented disruptions of the Democrats publicly “trashing” their nominee in incumbent President Joe Biden before replacing him with Harris and the prevalence of misinformation during that election caused a break in the model, Lichtman said.

Misinformation will continue to be a concern in elections going forward, but Lichtman remains hopeful for other great presidents after Trump’s term ends.

“After a period of weak and failed presidencies, you often get a great president,” Lichtman said.

“I'm always the optimist. One thing I've learned from the study of history: at times when things have seemed most bleak for the country, somehow we've turned the corner and come out of the darkness.”

Every red state is the same story of, the Republican governors are trying to ban anybody from studying sociology, film studies, anything like that, roll back on tenure. 

I went to Yale, and I’m following the various colleges and how the administrators are trying to fight, trying to defund or threaten any college. But you’re at Rutgers, so public college, blue state. So what’s the story been like there for you, and schools like that?

Wolfson: Yeah, I think even safe, relatively safe public blue state universities, when Trump first got into office, when he was, like, running around bull in a china shop and trying to knock over everything in his way, they were even scared, and they were like, Let’s just keep our heads down. Anybody who has DEI on their website, talking about diversity, equity, and inclusion, or critical race theory, you’re going to scrub that, right? And so—

Bacon: Not get fired, but scrub that from your website. There’s a difference between keeping your job and just, you know—

Wolfson: Yeah, you don’t get fired, but you’re going to scrub it from your website, and we’re going to keep our heads down.

And unfortunately, the thing about our universities and colleges and the leadership of them is that they have been caught in a pretty rough bind. And so I’m not happy with them, but I’m sympathetic to them. And the rough bind is this, right? You’re the president of Columbia University, and Donald Trump says to you, Look, I’m snatching $400 million out of your biomedical research infrastructure, for research you’re doing on diabetes and Alzheimer’s and X, Y, and Z, because there is antisemitism in the university—which I’m not going to substantiate, but I’m going to say it’s there. 

And so you’re the president, and you’re forced into a bind, and the bind is this: do I fight for higher education as a whole, right, and protect the institutional autonomy of Columbia University? Or do I fight for the financial wellbeing of Columbia University? And so it was a hard bind they were caught in. 

But unfortunately, the majority of the leadership of our universities—not the entirety, but the majority—made the choice to their fiduciary responsibility of their institution over their responsibility to higher education and democracy writ large. And so again, he caught them in a tough bind. He’s a bully. And unfortunately, though, we saw far too many kneel to that dynamic.

Bacon: You said more endorsements are coming. So I’d be curious what you mean by that, because my guess is the Democrat running in Alaska who didn’t want Kamala Harris’s endorsement may not be dying for yours either, candidly. So I’d be curious, is it governors, senators, mayors? Is it swing states?

Wolfson: Yeah, I’ll tell you what we’re looking at, a state where it’s very obvious. I think we’re mostly going to—not entirely, we may engage in state races, but we’ll mostly engage in federal races this time around, as we’re building up our muscles, learning to do this. And so there are really two criteria we’re looking at. 

One is swing states where we have a lot of density and could actually maybe potentially impact a race, where the candidate is speaking some of our language. They don’t have to be perfect, but they have to speak some of our language, and they can’t denigrate higher education.

That’s one category, of either Congress or congressional races, senatorial races. And then the other set of races are going to be in probably safe districts, where the people are really coming out and making a free public system central to their vision of a democratic society. And so those would be champions, right? 

People who are going to champion higher ed, talk about free public higher education as critical moving forward, an end to contingency, fully funded HBCUs, MSIs, fully funded biomedical research infrastructure. Those are the things we want. An end to student debt. And then the other half will be places where we can actually impact a race and project some power.

Bacon: Do you have two or three you’re considering you can name, or you want to stay away from that right now?

Wolfson: I’m going to stay away from it now, because I don’t want to get in front of my members.

Bacon: Of course. And does it matter if your local endorses, or is it set up that way where the locals—

Wolfson: Absolutely matters. We will not be going and stepping on our locals. We will be working with them and growing through with them. So we have locals. We, AAUP’s a pretty interesting beast, because we have 600 campuses where we have membership. And we have about 100 of them, we have collective bargaining rights. And so 100 campuses, more or less, we have collective bargaining rights, but that makes up 40 some odd thousand faculty members in AAUP. 

And then on the other 500 campuses, we don’t have collective bargaining rights. We have what you would call advocacy chapters, where they don’t get to negotiate, which is spread across 500 campuses, and it’s about another 20,000 members. And our locals have been endorsing candidates for office for decades upon decades. But our advocacy chapters haven’t.

Bacon: What percentage of university faculty are in AAUP?

Wolfson: I don’t know. That’s a good question. I would say it’s probably, overall, with the unionization rates in higher ed around 20, 25 percent. And faculty are so hard to enumerate now, because so many are temporary adjunct faculty. It’s a good question, and I should know the answer to that, but I don’t. But 20 to 25 percent of overall higher ed workers are unionized.

Bacon: You’ve been hinting at, and you’ve been saying, “I’m going to talk about our vision.” So what’s your vision for higher ed? You mention HBCUs, you mention free public, but lay out, what does AAUP see as what it wants higher education to look like in the United States?

Wolfson: Yeah. Our vision overall is that a robust democracy demands a robust free public higher education system, right?

Bacon: Does that mean free for everybody? Free for most students? What does that free mean? What do you want?

Wolfson: For me, it should be a universal right. I think we would have to win over a question of means testing with some of our allies who are elected. But to me, I want it to be universal.

Bacon: Like a universal public library.

Wolfson: Yes. And I really want to go back and fix the 1.8 trillion in debt that our students owe. But really, I think for us, there’s this vision of education and higher education as a central, if not the central, pillar to a healthy and robust democracy, where people are learning, where we’re engaging in critical questions, where if you get laid off at 35 as a lawyer, because now people are having Claude write their contracts that you could go back and you could get re-educated and find a way forward, and our universities become a place to support and grow through that very difficult time, which I think is coming. And I think we should really be honest about that. 

And so to me, it’s not a laundry list of, we want a free public system, we want the sort of investment through wealth taxes that enable that system. We want fully funded HBCUs and MSIs and HSIs, minority-serving institutions and Hispanic-serving institutions, and also tribal colleges and universities. But we also really want a robust research infrastructure. The great post-World War II deal in the United States that really drove our innovation was a partnership between the federal government and colleges and universities. 

And the deal was that we pay the universities and colleges, we have labs, we develop those labs, but the federal government funds critical research. And it’s the reason why—we don’t have a great healthcare system, it’s not good for the majority of us, but what we do have is the greatest healthcare research and innovation, and it comes out of our colleges and universities.

Our pharmaceutical companies would not do the primary research necessary that enables the breakthroughs that come, whether it’s cancer, Alzheimer’s, or any other number of things, Ozempic. They wouldn’t do the primary research necessary, because they don’t see the primary research as a return on investment. And so we need that relationship to grow. A thick, heavily funded research infrastructure, not only for healthcare, but for all untold number of things, and a place that’s a learning society. So that’s the real vision that we have. And I really believe we’re biting off our nose to spite our face when we undermine our great public education system as a public good, whether it’s K-12 or higher education.

And so that’s a vision for the society we have, which I would counter to the vision that Trump is putting out. The vision Trump is putting out, and his administration, is one that says—what did he say, six months ago? “I can’t pay for people’s early childhood learning. But what I can pay for is more bombs.” And that’s not the society I believe in. It’s not even the United States I was born into. And the United States—I was born in the ‘70s, I’m not going to say it was some great place for equity and diversity and for the working class, et cetera. 

But what I can say is, it wasn’t cruel like it is today. The cruelty wasn’t this externalized. And so I really think we want to fight for a learning society. We want to make public education free. We want debt-free pathways for people who go to private universities. And we want to build a society, rebuild in the ashes of what this president has done, in a way that’s good for all of us.

Bacon: Todd Wolfson, I’m excited about what you’re doing. Thanks for doing it. Thanks for joining me. Where can people find your thoughts and your work?

Wolfson: Go to aaup.org, please. And if you’re anywhere in higher education, please join us. Whatever campus, we want to build with you. We want to fight for your issues on your campuses, and we want to build with our students, all the students across this country, and staff, and build a system that reflects the greatness of our democracy.

Bacon: Todd, thanks for joining me. I appreciate it. Good to see you.

Wolfson: Thank you, Perry. I really appreciate it.

Bacon: Bye-bye.

news.title: Republicans keep losing because they won’t take hostages
news.text:
By now, most Americans have figured out that the push for the SAVE America Act is performative — perhaps even more than the usual Washington standards.

Republicans have a closing window of unified control of the House, Senate, and White House. Yet the structural advantages Democrats spent decades building remain largely untouched outside temporary executive action. The SAVE America Act is one way to answer that problem with basic election rules such as voter ID and limits on mail-in voting.

John Thune understands leverage perfectly well. It is time for Republicans who say they want this bill to pass to prove they do, too.

Elections remain vulnerable to the same disputes over identification, mail voting, and administration that Republicans have spent years denouncing, while other institutional fights — immigration enforcement and reform of the FBI among them — remain unfinished. If Republicans lose unified control without locking in durable changes, a future Democrat administration can reverse much of what has been done by executive order.

Despite what the D.C. consultant class says, Republican success in the midterms will hinge on base motivation. Voters need something to vote for. Democrats are already portraying Republicans as the party of their own DEI: data centers, the Epstein class, and the Iran war.

Fair or not, those are political anchors. Without a positive agenda, the charge will stick.

The consultant class responds with the usual sermon about unity, which in practice means: Get in line and do what leadership says. But voters do not want WWE. They want UFC.

The Republican Party is already in an internal fight over what it will become after Trump, and only one side seems willing to use leverage. Some will call that destructive infighting. But the fight is already happening, and it will shape the party for decades. The question is not whether Republicans should have an internal struggle. It’s whether conservatives intend to participate in it as effectively as the senators and institutions working against them.

Recent Senate fights make the point. Republicans have held up ICE funding to block an Anti-Weaponization Fund and delayed Attorney General Todd Blanche's confirmation. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) used leverage to extract millions for Alaska nonprofits.

Politics is, at bottom, the acquisition and use of leverage. The Senate's left-wing Republicans understand that. The right too often makes threats it will not carry out — and loses.

The real show is not on the Senate floor. It is in the bank accounts.

The money controlled by Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, led by Tim Scott (R-S.C.), explains more than another ideological taxonomy ever could. Hundreds of millions of dollars flow through leadership-aligned committees and outside groups from interests that want something from Washington. That money becomes both carrot and stick: protect friendly incumbents, discipline troublesome ones, and keep conservative senators talking rather than acting.

RELATED: Drain the swamp? Meet the refill.

 Sam Wolfe/Bloomberg via Getty Images

That’s how Thune and Scott can go on television praising the SAVE America Act while the leadership machine supports senators who stand in its way. My friends and I call this the head pat: Give conservatives a little rhetorical affection while making sure nothing they want actually happens. And it works. All the time.

The same network is lining up behind Senator Darline Graham Nordone (R-S.C.), rather than original SAVE America Act co-sponsor Ralph Norman. The scale is enormous. As of June 30, the Thune-aligned Senate Leadership Fund reported $238 million cash on hand, while its allied network, including One Nation, said it had raised more than half a billion dollars for the midterms. Those are obscene sums for a party that increasingly presents itself as the vehicle of working-class voters.

More important, the money is not politically neutral. It is a mechanism for deciding which senators get protected, which challengers get starved, and which legislative priorities receive serious attention.

Some of that war chest will protect senators most resistant to the SAVE America Act. Leadership gives them money and political lifelines while they deny the bill a vote. Those dollars do not come with strings attached for Republican voters. They come from donors and industries that need things from the Senate.

That is the leverage SAVE America Act supporters have ignored. If leadership can use money and floor time to reward compliance, conservatives can make leadership pay a price for blocking their priorities. Until they do, they have not begun to fight.

The absence of pressure is itself revealing. If leadership truly regarded passage of the SAVE America Act as a must-have priority, it would be using every institutional tool at its disposal to find votes and impose costs on holdouts. It is not.

The Senate made the problem obvious on August 8. Instead of forcing a vote on the full SAVE America Act, it took up a narrower photo-ID bill from Senator Jon Husted (R-Ohio). It failed 52-46. Then, that same morning, Thune filed cloture on the CLARITY Act crypto bill — a leadership priority that could consume much of the Senate's limited September floor time before the midterm campaign takes over.

Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), one of four Republicans who refuses to back the SAVE America Act, said the quiet part out loud: Unless its supporters find 60 votes, “they know it’s dead, and so all this is theater.” Thune says the Senate is “bound by arithmetic.” But arithmetic is not an alibi. Leadership chooses where to spend its money, floor time, and pressure.

So stop asking nicely.

RELATED: How Kamala Harris accidentally sold the SAVE America Act

 Christian Bruna/Getty Images

Senate leadership routinely holds unrelated priorities hostage to get what it wants. Republicans who actually want the SAVE America Act should do the same. When the Senate returns in September, it will face a college sports bill, Thune's CLARITY Act, and the National Defense Authorization Act. Those are leverage points.

A team sport works only if everyone is playing the same sport, wearing the same jersey, on the same field. Senate leadership is not behaving like it is on your team. Treating it as though it is only guarantees another round of speeches, cable hits, and failure.

The base needs to see a cage fight. Give the people what they want.

Refuse to hand leadership what it wants until the SAVE America Act gets an up-or-down vote at a 51-vote threshold. That is the same kind of hostage-taking the Senate’s left flank uses successfully. Thune understands leverage perfectly well. It is time for Republicans who say they want this bill to pass to prove they do, too.
