news.title: Trump made gas prices a political weapon. Now he’s downplaying the pain.
news.text:
Donald Trump once asked voters to judge his opponents by the sticker price at the gas pump. Now, he’s dismissing anger about those same prices under his watch even as the cost of living emerges as a top issue ahead of the midterms.Six months into the war with Iran, economic sentiment has shifted sharply against Republicans, including on that key metric, which voters previously pointed to as a singular area of relief before the war began.Labor Day, a symbolic campaign marker for when most voters tune into the upcoming fall elections, is just two weeks away, and the party’s options to turn around voters’ assessment of their handling of the economy are shrinking.

As Trump’s advisers and aides begin acknowledging frustrations with the cost of living, their top economic messenger– the president himself– continues to downplay them.

“For you to pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline, just remember you’re doing it so that a very evil country cannot have a [nuclear weapon],” Trump said earlier this month at a rally on Long Island. “So, remember that when you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4. It’s ok. I’ll never apologize, I did the right thing.”

“Affordability is a genuine issue, and Trump should be responding to it,” said Jason Sorens, a libertarian economist at the American Institute for Economic Research. “I don't think it would make sense for him to continue minimizing the affordability problem, and I think he has space to try to address it through reducing tariffs and trying to resolve the war.”Trump has said gas prices will “drop like a rock” as soon as hostilities end in the Middle East, but ceasefire agreements between the U.S. and Iran have repeatedly crumbled. Instability in the Strait of Hormuz stands to have lasting impacts on the oil market, according to analysts, months into a conflict that Americans were originally told would only last a few weeks.The average cost for a gallon of fuel is around $4.10 nationally, where the median price has settled for about a month now, according to AAA estimates as of Monday. Anger with energy prices extends beyond gas stations: voters are also vexed at the cost of everything from electricity to air conditioning.Mark Wolfe, who has worked in utility assistance for more than two decades, says that energy is “becoming a target for people's frustrations, and it's staying; it's sticking.”In his conversations with legislators and everyday Americans, he says he has never heard people, regardless of their income, express such ire toward energy companies. “Everyone's got one of these bills, and they see it,” Wolfe said. “They want to know someone is fighting for them.”Oil and gas companies have seen their profits surge in the wake of the war. Democrats in the U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee determined that Trump’s stock holdings of oil and gas companies contributed more than $15 million to his bottom line of $2 billion in income last year. In response to a request for comment, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said that the president’s stock portfolio is independently managed by a third-party financial institution using computer-based investment strategies.“Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold,” Ingle added.The president has put public pressure on retailers like Exxon and Chevrolet to lower prices for consumers, but he has rarely acknowledged that voters are struggling financially. In southwestern Ohio, Vice President JD Vance took a different approach on Friday, telling a local reporter that the administration is working a “great deal” on addressing higher prices.“The good news is gas prices got much higher than they are today,” said Vance, referencing the fact that prices were as high as $4.55 this summer. “It's something the Iranians have explicitly made part of their strategy in this particular conflict, so we're working on it very hard to try to get that relief.”

The president tapped into resentment about inflation in the 2024 election when he faced former President Joe Biden and later Vice President Kamala Harris. Under Biden’s administration, gas prices at their highest were $5 in 2022. Trump vowed to return them to under $2 if he won.“Thanks to Kamala's war on American energy, electricity prices are up 32 percent. Gasoline prices are up 50 percent and going higher,” Trump said in August 2024. “We hit $1.87” during Trump 1.0, he continued, “Harris and Biden blew it all up. If Kamala wins the election, the worst is yet to come.”By the time Biden and Harris left office, gas prices had dropped to $3.10 and continued to fall until President Trump launched the Iran war on Feb. 28 in concert with Israel.Republican lawmakers in Congress who were similarly outspoken about the cost of gas under the previous administration justified current prices as “a small price to pay” for the military campaign against Iran, echoing rhetoric used by Trump.The majority of Americans, 70%, disapprove of Trump’s stewardship of the economy and inflation, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll published earlier this month. Democrats held a slight edge over Republicans for which party voters’ trusted more to handle the cost of living, a reverse of historic trends.Trump told rallygoers in South Carolina on Friday that “as soon as” the U.S. stops Iran from securing a nuclear weapon, “oil is going to be down at lower than it was even just a little while ago.” It’s not clear what benchmark figure he was referring to.Last week, the president also dismissed fighting in the Strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed through prior to fighting in the waterway. Speaking alongside crypto leaders in the White House, Trump said the strait is “not going to be quite as important as it was in the past.”

The Trump administration has emphasized energy independence, but domestic oil prices are set based on the global market– making it impossible to fully detach from the constraints on oil supply worldwide.The White House has taken emergency measures to blunt the impact of the war on domestic oil prices, including tapping some 172 million barrels from the nation’s strategic reserves. Officials also suspended the Jones Act to permit foreign-flagged vessels to deliver goods to American ports, and waived U.S. sanctions on Russian oil.“President Trump and his entire energy team have taken decisive actions to mitigate disruptions to the energy markets and remain firmly committed to unleashing American energy dominance and cutting costs,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said in a statement.Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said attacks on oil refiners in Russia as a result of the war in Ukraine is also putting pressure on the oil market. As for an alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz which Trump aspires to achieve, it would likely “take years to fully address,” he says.Even if another ceasefire materializes, “all Iran would need to do to drive the uncertainty again” is “launch a couple of attacks here and there to keep up the risk element,” said De Haan. “There's no real way to plan for what tomorrow will bring.”

news.title: 'I've seen Donald Trump without make-up – he looks like an open can of Spam'
news.text: Donald Trump has suffered many unflattering comparisons during his long career in the spotlight. But being compared to an open can of Spam is surely a first. Financier turned political commentator Anthony Scaramucci served as Trump's White House communications director for an ill-fated 11-day stint at the beginning of the president's first term in office. It almost destroyed his career but he has since rebuilt his reputation as a successful political commentator, most notably on the podcast The Rest is Politics US. Having spent time at close quarters with Trump, Scaramucci is well placed to comment on what he is really like behind closed doors. And a critique from Scaramucci's mother, a make-up artist, on the president's cosmetics led to an incredible claim about his beauty regime. Speaking to The Times , he said: "She (his mother) hates Trump's make-up. It's like an orange bronzer he buys from a supply shop in the Bronx. He looks like an open can of Spam without make-up. "He puts it on in the morning. Sometimes he reapplies it at night. It's a tanner. He thinks it looks fantastic, by the way." Spam was introduced to America in 1937. The tinned meat quickly became popular and is notable for its distinctive light pink colour straight out of the can. It develops a golden-brown or reddish-brown hue when fried, grilled or baked. Rumours about Trump's skin tone have been swirling for decades. While most people believe he uses a bronzer, the president has previously answered his critics, blaming his colour on energy-efficient lightbulbs. During a House Republican retreat dinner in 2019, Trump said: "People said 'what's with the light bulb?' I said here's the story, and I looked at it. The bulb that we're being forced to use - no.1, to me, most importantly, the light's no good. I always look orange." But that hasn't stopped critics and comedians from handing him a series of derogatory nicknames, including 'Mango Mussolini' and 'Agent Orange'. Scaramucci was a long-time critic of Trump before he announced he was running for president back in 2015. During the following year's Republican Party presidential primaries, he endorsed first Scott Walker then Jeb Bush. But after both withdrew from the race, he joined Trump's campaign on his finance and then his transition team. He was later named the White House communications director in July 2017, but his time in the role proved to be short-lived. Scaramucci gave what he believed was an off-the-record chat with The New Yorker, in which he attacked White House colleagues Reince Priebus and Steve Bannon. He was promptly fired by Chief of Staff John Kelly, with Trump's approval. Scaramucci remained publicly loyal to Trump until the summer of 2019, after which he has returned to being a vocal critic of the president. He backed Joe Biden in 2020 and Kamala Harris in 2024. During his interview with the Times, Scaramucci claimed that no one he has met likes Trump - and that includes any of his relatives. He said: "I have yet to find a person that really likes Trump. Including all of his family members. Nobody likes him." He added that his wife Deidre is also not too keen on the president, saying: "My wife hates Trump almost as much as Melania. And if she was here, she would say more than Melania."
news.summary: A former colleague who has seen Donald Trump without his make-up says "he looks like an open can of Spam" before applying his bronzer - but the president "thinks it looks fantastic"

news.title: The Morning Briefing: SCOTUS Helps Preserve a Modicum of Sanity in Mail-In Ballot Madness
news.text:
Top O' the Briefing

Happy Tuesday, dear Kruiser Morning Briefing friends. The Sine Qua Non Sequitur is spending the day helping traveling Cesar Romero impersonators with some embroidery.

I want to thank Sarah for filling in for me on short notice while I dealt with some family stuff (my unscheduled days off are rarely for anything fun). It's good to be back even though I feel like I could nap for a fortnight. 

President Trump hasn't been getting any help from Republicans in the Senate in his efforts to make our elections a little more transparent and less susceptible to fraud. Senate Majority Leader John Thune isn't really leading anyone, preferring the invertebrate hand-wringing that was the hallmark of pre-Trump Republicans to anything that might help his party to win. 

The president likes results, and if he isn't getting them from Congress, he is willing to do what needs to be done via executive orders. That route, of course, often runs into problems with activist liberal judges and/or courts. Fortunately, the highest court in the land is still mostly conservative and will occasionally give Trump a helpful hand, which it did again yesterday.

This is from Matt:

The Supreme Court just handed President Trump a massive victory in the fight to secure America's elections. The justices cleared the way for his executive order restricting mail-in voting to move forward, and after months of Democrat officials trying to bury the policy in court, the administration finally has room to breathe.This is a big deal.The SAVE America Act is still stalled in the Senate, blocked by Democrats who aren’t even hiding the fact they have zero interest in verifying that voters are who they say they are. Trump's executive order just got a green light from the nation's highest court anyway. Election integrity doesn't have to die in the legislative graveyard to make progress.Trump signed the executive order, called "Ensuring Citizenship Verification And Integrity In Federal Elections," in March 2026. It directs his administration to build lists of eligible voters and orders the U.S. Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to people on those lists.

Anything to combat the fraud potential of vote-by-mail is helpful, and this is a good start. I'm a tough sell on this issue because I would prefer that the pool of people who are eligible to vote via the mail be drastically reduced. None of the measures discussed or proposed in recent years go far enough in my opinion. My baseline starts with state laws that allow all-mail elections being struck down. 

Because the Democrats won't be happy until all of our elections practically lawless free-for-alls that have myriad options for fraud to be introduced into the process, they lie about anything that pushes back on that agenda. I wrote last week that it is illegal to punch Dems who don't tell the truth about this stuff. As of this writing, it still is. 

My Twitchy colleague Doug P. collected some Dems' reactions to the ruling. Here's Granny Boxwine's hot take:

The right to vote is the foundation of our Democracy, and the Supreme Court’s decision allowing the President to move forward with this assault on that right is an insult to the vision of our founders.Trump’s attempt to seize control over Americans’ ability to vote by mail… https://t.co/rOvZQKwQ2p— Nancy Pelosi (@SpeakerPelosi) August 24, 2026

Ensuring that mail-in ballots are sent only to those who are eligible to vote isn't an "attempt to seize control" of, well, anything. In most cases, this could be written off as merely another example of Pelosi being nonsensical — she was tossing up word salads long before Kamala Harris — but her remarks are a variation on the theme of the responses from most Dem officials. 

Vote-by-mail features the least amount of election transparency and therefore offers the greatest potential for fraud, especially in states like California where every voter gets sent a ballot whether it was requested or not. When I lived in California, I was put on a permanent vote-by-mail list even though I'd never voted absentee or asked to be put on a list. Every election, I would fill out a provisional ballot and check a box requesting that I be removed from the list but I never was. Three years after I had moved back to Arizona, I was still on that list. 

The messier and more out of date that the voter rolls in a state are, the more ripe they are for election "anomalies," as they've become known by those who want to insist that election fraud is no big deal. The Democrats have no coherent reason to be opposed to clean voter rolls. Their levels of hysteria when responding to common sense measures like this only make them seem even more guilty of all the things that we accuse them of. 

Again, this is helpful, but there is a long way to go in order to fix the problems in our elections. The identification requirements in the SAVE Act would be a huge step in the right direction, but John Thune and the Mitch McConnell-esque GOP jellyfish might kill that because of reasons and feelings and stuff. 

President Trump will just have to keep firing up that executive order pen of his and seeing what survives the lefty courts gauntlet. Then maybe, just maybe, we can one day get some Republicans in Congress who won't be afraid to act like they've won an election after they've, you know, won an election.

news.title: Exclusive — North Macedonia's Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski: ‘We Strongly Support’ President Trump, United States
news.text:
WASHINGTON — North Macedonia’s Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski told Breitbart News exclusively that his country’s government is “strongly” supportive of American President Donald Trump’s government and policies on a number of fronts, from foreign policy to energy to geopolitics and more.

Mickoski told Breitbart News that his government formally backed Trump even before his comeback in the 2024 election, hosting Trump-campaign-aligned officials in North Macedonia in mid-2024 and then sending a formal delegation to Trump’s inauguration in early 2025.

“Even prior to him becoming President of the United States, some of the people which are part of his closest perimeter visited us even during the campaign when there was not too many European nations that believed that President Trump would become president,” Mickoski said in a nearly hourlong phone interview last week. “We were elected as a government in June 2024. Immediately after the NATO summit in D.C. in July 2024, a team of associates of President Trump visited us in the government and we were practically in that time the only government that received the members of the team of President Trump. Among them was Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, Devin Nunes, former member of the Congress, and of Macedonian origin Chris Pavlovski, the owner of Rumble. They visited us in the government, and we strongly conveyed a message of support for President Trump prior to him becoming president. Then, when he was elected as president, I was invited during the inauguration ceremony and a delegation of the Macedonian government visited D.C. in that time so we conveyed our message of support and willingness for increasing of future cooperation. Practically, we are fully aligned with all resolutions in United Nations, and we supported them in the past two years a lot of times when it comes to the Iran issue, Venezuela, Cuba issue, and so on and so forth. Also, we are in a very strong communication with Ambassador Ric Grenell. We are discussing about the future potential cooperation in energy with the Ambassador of the United States in Greece, Ms. [Kimberly] Guilfoyle. We are talking about American LNG trade potential in the region. We are trying to promote economical interest in the region, and we strongly do that. We are the pivotal point of American interests in the Balkans, and we are a strong pillar of support of American interests in the Balkans. So, practically, without any doubt, we stand next to our strategical partners, the United States’s and President Trump’s policy, and we strongly support them.”

Mickoski said that Trump’s support in his nation is very high, higher than anywhere else in Europe, and that he would be happy to welcome Trump to North Macedonia should the American president’s schedule allow for a trip.

“Seeing that the polls of President Trump are the highest in my country, so Macedonian citizens are supporting very decisively President Trump’s administration, and when I’m saying that the polls are highest, I’m meaningful because I’m following the polls, and I know that his credibility among Macedonian citizens is absolutely huge, and without any doubt, keen to invite him,” Mickoski said. “I will be very keen to host him at the highest level. He will enjoy the support of Macedonian citizens. When he will have available time slot in his schedule we will be very keen to host him if he decides to visit the region, because as I said, like not so many allies in Europe, we are the country without any doubt for support when it comes to the President Trump administration, even much more longer time ago and prior to him becoming president officially, when there were not too many countries in Europe believing that he would defeat Kamala Harris during the presidential race.”

North Macedonia was also one of the first countries to negotiate a trade deal with the United States after Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs, and Mickoski said he hopes more deals can get signed in the coming weeks when he visits the United States for the United Nations General Assembly in New York. He said he hopes to visit the White House to see Trump or to see him on the sidelines of the UNGA in New York.

“Yes, we negotiated one year ago, I think it was, when we started our negotiations with President Trump’s administration, and we reached we reached a compromise,” Mickoski said. “We impose zero custody rate for the United States products for importing in the territory of my country, and so vice versa. We’ve got zero tariffs when it comes to the exporting Macedonian products to the United States. So practically, more or less, we have common ground, and I think that soon from now, probably there is a chance now during the UNGA to have an official meeting, either in White House or wherever, to sign this bilateral treaty between both of countries. So I think that this will add a value on the relations of both countries.”

He is hoping for even more cooperation between the U.S. and North Macedonia in the coming months.

“Since I’m traveling for UNGA this year—for the United Nations General Assembly—maybe it will be a good opportunity to sign this bilateral treaty either in the White House or in the Department of State, whichever works,” Mickoski said. “For us, it’s very important, and I think that for the United States it is very important because through us, by increasing our economical cooperation, this will increase bilateral cooperation as well. Even our bilateral cooperation is at the highest point ever, historically speaking. But by signing this bilateral treaty, everything will be much more easier for both countries. So, the United States has a very strong ally in the Balkans. I know that they appreciate very much what we are doing for our partnership. But with this bilateral treaty, we will make our bilateral partnerships much more stronger and much more feasible in terms of economical cooperation in the future, and this will open the gates for U.S. exports and investors to have a much more ambitious and much more meaningful role not only in the Balkans but also in Europe generally speaking.”

Both Grenell and Guilfoyle, top Trump officials, spoke highly of Mickoski ahead of the Breitbart News interview with him—and Mickoski likewise spoke highly of both of them. Mickoski made clear that North Macedonia very much so backs Trump and the United States on key matters even when it’s politically inexpedient to do so—including voting lockstep with the United States at the United Nations.

“When America needed allies to take positions practically, my country did not hide in the crowd, which is very important,” Mickoski told Breitbart News. “We stood with the United States very quickly, clearly, and consistently, including when practically doing so carries a political cost. That was for us very important because friends are when some others are not such devoted friends as they are pretending to be in the peaceful times. So practically, when President Trump needed our support in United Nations voting declarations, which are based on the interests of the President Trump’s administration, we gave our no-doubtless support without any reservations unlike with some other stakeholders. So that was a clear message of support, and we will continue to do so in the future.”

It is not just bureaucratic institutions where the North Macedonians are providing support. United States Air Force jets are using North Macedonia’s airports—in the heart of the Balkans in Eastern Europe—as a strategic location near the Middle East. Mickoski told Breitbart News he is proud to lend support to the United States in the war with Iran.

“The American Air Force is using our airports, so every day American Air Force aircraft are landing and departing from our airports,” Mickoski said. “So some of them are using our airports for parking, for taking a rest a little bit, and going back to the Gulf. We have an open sky for American aircrafts, military aircrafts, and we are proud to and we are on disposal to provide such support for the American Air Force, of course.”

North Macedonia is just north of Greece, and just south of Serbia, right in the heart of the Balkans—Albania borders North Macedonia to the west, and Bulgaria to the east.

Mickoski described his nation as being on the “front line” of an “invisible battlefield” in an emerging economic war between the west—the United States and Europe—and the far east, in China.

“I will try to describe a little bit the geo-strategical position of my country, which is unfortunately a landlocked country—which might be considered as a small disadvantage,” Mickoski said. “We are a couple of tens of kilometers far from the sea, but unfortunately we are not exposed to the sea since something from the past. However, we are a crossroads of two very important pan-European corridors, but not pan-European only. They are important for the world as well. I’m talking about corridor eight and corridor ten. What is the purpose of both corridors? Corridor eight is connecting the Adriatic and Ionian Sea with the Black Sea, and corridor ten is connecting the Mediterranean and Aegean Sea with Central Europe. Corridor eight is very important due to the fact that immediately when the war in Ukraine will be over, and when the reconstruction of Ukraine will start, this corridor eight will be very important for the supply chain, and practically this will make a shorter supply chain and the cost of delivery will be much lower. When it comes to the corridor ten, it’s worth mentioning that corridor ten, as I said, is connecting the Mediterranean, although I mean Aegean Sea with the Central European countries like Hungary, Austria, and so on and so forth. Practically, we are here, hypothetically speaking, we are at the front line of this invisible battlefield. When I’m talking about an invisible battlefield, I’m talking about the Chinese interest in this part of Europe, European interests on their own soil, and the American interests. Why we are at the front line of the invisible battlefield? Because now everything that comes from the east, all raw materials, all products, are used in two ports in Europe, the ports of Rotterdam and Hamburg. China acquired two ports in Greece, Piraeus port, and they are a shareholder into the Thessaloniki port as well. When I’m talking about Piraeus port, I’m talking about complete ownership of the port. So practically, they’re expanding the capacity of the port. Why? Because they will need, they want to use Piraeus port for harboring vessels—and practically they would like to connect these Piraeus ports with Central Europe which will make the supply chain shorter between 18 and 22 days. So you can imagine what 18 and 22 days nowadays means in terms of costs and in terms of increasing the competitiveness and increasing the maneuvering space and decreasing of a price.”

The North Macedonians have formally made clear to the world they side with the United States, and they are also trying to gain entrance—a decades-long goal—into the European Union. Mickoski warned of China’s rising influence in the region, particularly through its efforts to buy and fund ports in Greece—particularly the Piraeus port. As Breitbart News has previously reported, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Piraeus port in Greece just outside Athens and called it China’s “dragon’s head” in Europe. Greek Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis and Guilfoyle, the U.S. Ambassador to Greece, spoke in interviews for that story laying out how the United States has responded by funding a port of its own in Greece—but Mickoski warned that the long-term goals of the Chinese are to “swamp” the markets of western countries with companies controlled by the Chinese Communist Party. He cited as an example Chinese electric automaker BYD’s growth in Hungary.

“China will use Piraeus port to export products and raw materials and to deploy all of them to Central Europe, for example, BYD,” Mickoski told Breitbart News. “I don’t know whether you have this information. BYD commissioned a production facility in Hungary worth $10 billion, and literally now BYD swamps up competition when we are talking about electric vehicles in the European market. So the number one seller in the European market now is BYD. Imagine what will happen in the future if we allow China to connect Piraeus with Central Europe. Literally, they will swamp up competition from the European market, and they will dominate, and they will conquer the European market. So the only puzzle which is missing in the mosaic is the territory of my country. Why? Because they are building a fast railway which is connecting Budapest via Belgrade with the northern border of my country with Serbia and an important fast railway in Greece, so practically the only section which is missing in the mosaic is the section which is crossing on the territory of my country, connecting the northern border with Serbia and southern border with Greece. So that’s why I’m saying that we are at the front line of an invisible economical battlefield.”

North Macedonia does not seek hostilities with China, and respects China’s One China policy, but Mickoski explained that the priorities of his country are working with the United States to advance freedom on the world stage.

“We respect the principle of one China without any doubt, but at the meantime, our strategic partner is the United States, together with our allies in NATO and with our partners in the EU,” Mickoski said. “But our utmost priority are relations with our strategic partner, the United States, and the current President Trump administration. So this is our pathway forward, and we will follow our pathway forward in the future.”

North Macedonia has also been trying for many years to join the European Union, and has faced issues with disputes between North Macedonia and both Greece and Bulgaria with French President Emmanuel Macron even vetoing its induction at one point. Mickoski said the “second milestone for my country” after working with the United States as a first priority “is to be a part of the EU.”

“To be a part of the EU is good for plenty of reasons for my country and for the citizens of my country. Why? Because we are talking about increasing the security and increasing the resilience of the region overall,” Mickoski said. “We started our journey two and a half decades ago. It was 2000 when we signed a stabilization and association agreement with the European Union. Then, together with Croatia in 2005, we’ve become officially candidate countries to be a part of the EU. In 2008, from the European Commission, we’ve got the first positive report for starting the negotiations but unfortunately since then our hurdles and our challenges started. So practically, it was first the name dispute with our south neighbor Greece, and now we have a dispute with our eastern neighbor Bulgaria, and all those disputes are somehow connected with our identity. I don’t know whether you knew that information, but we are facing a lot of challenges since we’ve become an independent state from the former Yugoslavia. So if we go back three and a half decades ago, I must flag out a couple of very important pieces of information. We changed our flag. We changed our currency. In the meantime, we changed our constitution two times, and finally we changed our constitutional name. According to a lot of, I would say, bureaucrats from Brussels and from all over the world, it’s supposed to be the last thing that we did. But unfortunately they betrayed us and they lied to us. Immediately after our change of our constitution, French President Macron imposed a veto. He requested a change of methodology of negotiations, and when the new methodology for negotiations was adjusted, then unfortunately our eastern neighbor came to the scene and they asked from us to change our constitution. So practically, we are now in a very, I would say, critical situation, and very funny situation. In one multilateral organization, we are allies with Bulgaria, with our eastern neighbor. I’m talking about NATO. And in another multilateral organization, European Union, we have the same allies from NATO imposing constraints for us and imposing a veto, which is not a very, I would say, friendly gesture. Those are the double standards and unanimity rule within the EU itself. They can’t understand that our membership in the EU is strategical for NATO. As I said, from plenty of reasons, among them is resilience and security. So they are weakening the south and eastern flank of NATO by constraining us to become a part of the EU, because as economically much more stronger is my country that makes much more resilient the eastern flank of NATO—and we will be able to modernize in a much quicker way our armed forces and invest more into the corridors which are important for logistical purposes of NATO. So there are plenty of reasons why we need to be a part of the EU, and this is the reason plus for the United States and President Trump’s administration to support us in this manner.”

North Macedonia earlier this year signed a “strategic dialogue” with the United States, and Mickoski is hopeful this will expand beyond that into even more concrete economic cooperation between the two nations.

“We want to turn the strategic dialogue into the present Trump-style diplomacy, with fewer bureaucratic processes and more concrete deliverables in security, energy technology, and infrastructure, trade, and investments,” Mickoski said. “This is our milestone, and we signed a lot of MOUs. I think that there is big progress. DFC [the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation] is financing one very important project, a mine project. We we have probably the biggest depot of antimony. So there is a big Australian and Canadian investment in the country, and the U.S. is financially supporting that kind of investment. So practically, we will excavate antimony in my country, and we will deploy that critical mineral to the United States. Later, the United States will use this critical mineral for producing military equipment. So practically, we have very, very, very strong ties created with the strategic dialogue.”

North Macedonia is also, Mickoski said, very supportive of Trump’s efforts to get NATO allies to spend more on their national defense. He said North Macedonia is already north of 2 percent of its GDP on defense spending with a plan to get as high as 3.5 percent—with an additional 1.5 percent of GDP spending on critical infrastructure projects to be used by NATO forces.

“Yes, you are absolutely right, and practically we are in the first half of the group,” Mickoski said, the groups referenced being most of Europe which is already spending more on defense versus a small minority which is not. “We are now above the threshold of 2 percent when it comes to the military expenditures. We are, I think, that we are in the first half of the group, and we prepared a scenario on how to reach 3.5 percent up to 2032. On top of that, we have 1.5 percent of our GDP investments into our critical infrastructure, which will be used by NATO South and Eastern flanks. So practically, this is the exact idea of President Trump: 5 percent overall, 3.5 percent military, typically military expenditures, and 1.5 percent investments and expenditures into critical infrastructure which will be used by NATO forces, like railways and highways and so on and so forth. So practically, we are fully aligned with this idea of President Trump, and we strongly support this idea.”

Mickoski said he was very proud of the speeches that both Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered to Europeans early last year and early this year, respectively. He also referenced a speech Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick gave as well with similar warnings for Europe. Mickoski said he may have been the only European leader clapping for Vance’s speech to the Munich Security Conference.

“I was in the room during both speeches but also for the not officially revealed speech of Howard Lutnick, Secretary of Commerce, during the official dinner at the Davos World Business Forum this year. So practically, the two of them had similar speeches conveyed by a different tone, but more or less the messages were the same,” Mickoski said. “Let me start from Vice President Vance’s speech at the Munich Security Conference back in early 2025. So, according to my humble opinion, I’m not flattering here. But I think that that was a very sovereign and very straightforward speech with a lot of frank messages, real policy-making messages, and very realistic messages. Absolutely, you’re right—probably, I was the only person in the room who was clapping with the hands and trying to support the messages that he conveyed during his speech, and I strongly believe that that kind of sovereign speech is the future of humanity. Otherwise, we will lose our identity and credibility, which is something in the contrary of our policy-making process and probably in the contrary of the United States and President Trump’s policy-making process. More or less the same was rhetoric delivered this year with Rubio, but as you said, with a different tone, and maybe the situation among the European allies is changed a little bit. Now, according to my humble opinion, I think that the messages that are coming from the other side of the ocean are considered much more seriously, and I think that our allies in Europe are trying to remain with very close ties with the President Trump administration nowadays, because to be honest and frank, the United States Armed Forces and administration of President Trump is providing the security umbrella for our continent. I think that you can’t play double games and you can’t enjoy double standards. So practically, either you are a liar or not. So this is not a buffet breakfast table. ‘I would like this to eat and that to eat, not that, I don’t like this and I would like that.’ So practically, this is a process. Either we are all together, or we are alone. It’s like a chain. The chain is solid enough and strong enough, as much as the weakest part of the chain is strong. So practically, if one part of the chain is destroyed, then probably the chain will not exist anymore. So this is the way how, according to my understanding, this is the way how our allies in Europe are thinking at this moment, so we must be together and we must stay together with the President Trump administration because as I said President Trump’s administration is providing too many reasons to support that administration. For us, this is inevitable process as a country, but I think that most of our European allies consider that this is inevitable process as well.”

North Macedonia is also going to be a huge part of the so-called “Vertical Corridor” which will ship American LNG up from Greece through pipelines into Central Europe and Ukraine. Mickoski said there are multiple inter-connectors his country is currently building on its southern border with Greece and on its northern border with Serbia, to help move the project along quickly.

“Now we are building inter-connectors that will connect my country with the south, in Greece, and practically that pipeline will leap all over to the LNG terminal Alexandroupolis,” Mickoski said. “We have four slots reserved at the LNG terminal in Alexandroupolis. So practically, in this inter-connector, this pipeline, this Alexandroupolis terminal will become more effective, but it will not be enough. That’s why we are investing into the northern inter-connector pipeline that will connect our national pipeline with the Serbian national pipeline. In that regard, Alexandroupolis—from Greece to Macedonia and Serbia, all over to Central Europe, to Hungary and to Austria. The capacity of the pipeline is between three and six BCM [billion cubic meters] annually, which will make this pipeline real, tangible competition to the Russian assets in the region. So practically, this is the only project which is the transit-able competitor of the Russian assets in the region, and this is the project that might make doable the ambitions of the President Trump administration for exporting the LNG through Alexandroupolis terminal to Central Europe, and we are developing northern inter-connector by our own financial resources from our budget. But when it comes to the south inter-connector, we are using European funding. So practically, at the beginning of 2028, if everything goes according to the plan that we have foreseen, we will connect Alexandroupolis terminal with Central Europe.”

Mickoski is also trying to build multiple hydropower plants to help generate lots of electricity that and to help water flows in North Macedonia.

“Those two hydropower plants are very important for all of us, but not only for the country and not only for producing electricity,” he said. “Bearing in mind climate changes and global heating, I think that the region will need the additional two reservoir supporters. My country has a wonderful perspective, and this is a magnificent, amazing environment for developing those kind of hydropower plants with the high dams, with a big installed capacity, and this is the only reason why we would like to develop those two hydropower plants first to secure our water supply for the region, and second for the irrigation, and then as a third priority producing electricity—although we are talking about one terawatt hour electricity annually, which is a super big amount of electricity for the size of a country like ours. This is a super big amount of electricity.”

The extra electricity, he said, will help North Macedonia build data centers to harness the power of artificial intelligence and he is holding meetings currently with the CEO of Rumble—the major video streaming platform—Chris Pavlovski, whose ancestors are Macedonian, to talk about building them in his country.

“Everybody now is talking about AI, about artificial intelligence, and practically artificial intelligence without data centers—it’s so you can’t drive your data centers without having a sustainable supply of electricity,” Mickoski said. “This is the only way we are able to drive data centers and how we are able to work on artificial intelligence. Chris is investing a lot with his partners in Europe. I know that they acquired one big company in Germany, and since he has super big patriotic feelings for the country of his roots, of his family’s roots, he wants to invest in Macedonia, and I will meet him this weekend, so we will be able to talk more about his potential investments and the investments of his colleagues into the data centers and what we are able to provide for them. So, practically, when we are talking about with those two hydropower plants, we are talking about the project with the amount of $1.5 billion, and also when we are talking about data centers, we are talking about complete American investment, and we’ll be working to provide all necessary incentives what we are able to provide for them to make that investment doable in the future.”

news.title: Former Kansas Sen. Nancy Kassebaum remembered as trailblazer
news.text:
Former Sen. Nancy Kassebaum Baker, who broke multiple barriers for women in the Senate, has died at the age of 94. 

The Kansas Republican died of natural causes in hospice care on Aug. 21, her son Bill Kassebaum confirmed to The New York Times.

Memorials came in from across the political spectrum in Kansas. Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly said in a statement that “Kansas lost part of its soul” with Kassebaum’s death. 

Kassebaum was the first woman to represent her state in the Senate and the first woman to lead a major committee, taking the gavel of the Labor and Human Resources panel in 1995 during the 104th Congress. 

Kassebaum was a relative political neophyte when she was first elected to the Senate in 1978. Her only prior political experience had been serving on the school board of Maize, Kan. — pop. 785, at the time — and as an aide for one year to GOP Sen. James B. Pearson. 

But her roots in Kansas politics ran deep: Her father, Alfred M. Landon, was a governor of Kansas and the 1936 Republican presidential nominee, who lost to Franklin D. Roosevelt in a landslide. 

When Pearson retired, Kassebaum — then Nancy Landon Kassebaum — ran to succeed him, buoyed by name recognition and TV ads featuring her father. She comfortably defeated Democratic former Rep. William R. Roy.

Kassebaum was the lone woman in the Senate when she was sworn in later that year after being appointed to serve out the last days of Pearson's term, upon his resignation on Dec. 23, 1978. She remained the only female senator until Florida Republican Paula Hawkins joined the chamber in early 1981.

She brought a noted independent streak to her office, breaking with her party on key issues, including gun control and abortion. After the 1994 Republican Revolution, Kassebaum helped strike welfare overhaul provisions from the GOP’s “Contract With America” agenda that would have denied benefits to unmarried teenage mothers and the children of welfare recipients. 

Kassebaum speaks to reporters in May 1993 as first lady Hillary Clinton and Sens. Harris Wofford of Pennsylvania and Tom Harkin of Iowa look on. (Laura Patterson/CQ Roll Call)

Her own legislative contributions include the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, with Massachusetts Democrat Edward M. Kennedy, which made it harder for health insurers to deny coverage based on pre-existing conditions and prior group coverage. 

She took a more conservative stance on other issues, opposing proposals to raise the minimum wage and require businesses to provide unpaid family and medical leave, saying she felt it was wrong to mandate benefits — to the chagrin of Democrats who mainly knew her through her moderate social stances. "I always feel like the skunk at the picnic on this issue," she said at the time. 

Kassebaum’s knack for mediating disagreements helped her earn a reputation as a bridge-builder, while her mild manner sometimes verged on discomfort with being a public figure. "Someday I'm going to hit someone over the head for calling me diminutive and soft-spoken," she once said. "But I am."

She was a trailblazer in smaller ways, as well. Irked by unwritten rules around what women could wear on the Senate floor in the early 1990s, Kassebaum and Sen. Barbara A. Mikulski, D-Md., staged a protest of sorts, wearing trousers to a weekend session and encouraging female staffers to do the same. Pantsuits soon became the norm. 

In 1996, Kassebaum married Howard H. Baker Jr., the former Senate Republican leader from Tennessee, creating a true Washington power couple. That same year, she announced her retirement from the Senate, saying she had wanted to spend more time on other challenges, “including the challenge of being a grandmother.” The couple lived for a time in Japan, where Baker served as ambassador under President George W. Bush. 

Kassebaum poses with fellow female senators at her retirement party in 1996. From left, Sens. Kay Bailey Hutchison of Texas, Barbara A. Mikulski of Maryland, Carol Moseley-Braun of Illinois and Sheila Frahm of Kansas. (CQ Roll Call file photo)

Toward the end of her life, Kassebaum’s ties to the Republican Party under President Donald Trump had begun to fray. She called for Trump’s impeachment after the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, The Washington Post reported, and endorsed several Democrats, including Kelly for governor and Kamala Harris for president. 

Members of the current Kansas delegation in Congress fondly remembered Kassebaum over the weekend, including Republican Rep. Derek Schmidt, who worked for Kassebaum for five years on Capitol Hill. 

“Senator Kassebaum introduced this kid from a small Southeast Kansas town to opportunities for public service I had not known possible,” Schmidt said on social media.

GOP Sen. Jerry Moran said he campaigned for her in multiple Senate races, calling her a “friend and encourager” who “was never afraid to challenge me in our conversations.”

“Senator Kassebaum’s time in public service embodied the institution of the U.S. Senate at its best,” Moran said.

news.title: Black Dems to Talarico: Why Won't You Show Us the Money?
news.text:
Or so analysts keep insisting. On the other hand, the fundamentals on the ground in Texas, especially among black voters, indicate a far different outcome. Former Kamala Harris staffer Ashley Etienne told Meet the Press this weekend that the only way for a Democrat to win a statewide election is for the black vote to "overperform." After visiting Houston, Etienne isn't feeling anything close to that level of enthusiasm for Talarico, in part because Talarico still hasn't shown them the money:

Former Kamala Harris staffer Ashley Etienne says far-Left Democrat James Talarico is underperforming with Black Democrats:"The only way you win [Texas] as a Democrat is if you overperform with black voters...they are concerned that there's mild enthusiasm among black voters." pic.twitter.com/EL4diFLe6b— RNC Research (@RNCResearch) August 23, 2026

“Listen, my home state of Texas, we feel incredibly encouraged for two reasons,” Ashley Etienne, formerly the communications director for Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris, told “Meet the Press” host Kristen Welker on Sunday. “But the challenge is: the only way you win the state of Texas as a Democrat is if you overperform with Black voters.”“I just came back from Houston last night, meeting with operatives on the ground and state elected officials. They are concerned that there’s mild enthusiasm among black voters and that this $25 million that Talarico promised he was going to spend over a month ago has yet to start to flow,” she continued.

Wait ... what? Talarico supposedly has as much as $50 million on hand. His campaign promised to spend half of that in the black community almost exactly a month ago. Talarico has stepped up his pandering to black voters in the meantime, most recently in his mind-boggling decision to weigh in on the Karmelo Anthony appeal before evidence emerged of Anthony's criminal record and malevolent streak. Talarico has upped the ante, literally, with these voters, and he hasn't yet shown them the money?

Etienne says no one in Houston has seen evidence of it, and that Talarico's money advantage is about to go Tango Uniform anyway:

“The investments aren’t there yet. And then you couple that with the fact that Elon Musk said he’s going to spend nearly $200 million on these races, and Texas is a huge target for that. And you’ve got a problem with black voters in Texas: you’ve got 34% of black men voting for Donald Trump. So if you’re going to wait until Labor Day to start campaigning with black voters, you’re playing to lose.”

Donald Trump will be in Texas on Thursday for a rally and fundraiser for Paxton, too. His MAGA Inc PAC has over $400 million in cash even without Musk's pledge to kick in half as much directly to Republican campaigns. Musk has a particular interest in defeating Talarico, as the NY Post pointed out last week:

Elon Musk is likely to shell out nine-figure sums to help Republicans fend off Democrats in this year’s midterm elections — particularly in Texas, where GOP Senate hopeful Ken Paxton faces a massive fundraising disadvantage.Officials briefed on the matter told Wired that Musk is expected to spend between $100 million and $200 million to boost Republicans, though the precise amount could change.The Tesla and SpaceX boss is expected to focus his political war chest on voter turnout in competitive races, with the closely watched Texas contest between Paxton and Democrat James Talarico among the potential beneficiaries.

Democrats have tried to make Musk into a bete noire ever since he bought Twitter four years ago. On this point, though, they have a rational fear of his political intervention. Musk does a lot of business in Texas, and while members of the Senate don't have much direct impact on state business environments, Musk understands that a Talarico win in Texas might spark a political shift within the state, especially with weak-kneed Republicans in the state legislature. Musk almost certainly sees this race as a leading indicator for a potential retrenchment that will put his business interests at risk, and he will use his resources to protect against it – not to mention the necessity of blunting any progressive momentum nationwide. 

There is another nugget in this report that didn't get much attention, although I noted it in a Final Word at the time:

Talarico has raised $68.6 million through June 30, more than seven times the roughly $9.2 million hauled in by Paxton’s campaign, according to Federal Election Commission filings.The Democrat also held $21.5 million in cash at the end of June compared with just $1.8 million for Paxton, the filings showed.

That's still a big advantage for Talarico, campaign-on-campaign. However, it shows a massive burn rate that hasn't moved the needle yet even among the Texas Democrats' base, let alone the center of the state's electorate. It also suggests that the reason Talarico has not yet shown black voters the money is that he doesn't actually have $25 million to burn in relitigating the primaries against Jasmine Crockett. If that's the case, then Talarico will learn a lesson about expectation-setting and delivery in November.

Speaking of Crockett, she also insists that black voters won't turn out for Talarico. Crockett echoes Etienne about the enthusiasm gap, which has enormous implications for any Democrat running statewide in Texas:

💥NEW: Jasmine Crockett says black community isn't "EXCITED" about James Talarico💥"I personally don't feel like the excitement necessarily exists within the black community ... I don't feel like they're excited!"Crockett dominated Talarico in counties with large black… pic.twitter.com/GChJdaNUOd— Jason Cohen 🇺🇸 (@JasonJournoDC) August 21, 2026

Crockett dominated Talarico in counties with large black voting-age populations during the primary, according to a Reuters analysis.Texas also happens to be the state with the largest black population in the U.S. Talarico will need strong black turnout to have any shot at beating Ken Paxton.Comments like this from Crockett won't help.

These comments don't help, but also notably, neither Crockett nor Colin Allred appear inclined to help as well. These are the two most prominent black Democrats in the state, and their firm choices to stay on the sidelines send a clear signal to black voters in this race. Not that it may matter much; Allred did have enthusiastic-to-overperforming support from black voters in 2024 and still lost to Ted Cruz by nine points. There is zero chance that Talarico will get that level of support from black voters, and nearly zero chance of getting replacement levels of support from anywhere else in the Texas electorate. 

The only advantages Talarico has at the moment are cash and highly questionable polling. Expect both of those advantages to dissipate quickly after Labor Day, with or without Musk's contributions.

news.title: In Maine, Vance shouts out Susan Collins at vice presidential visit she skipped
news.text:
Vice President JD Vance used an appearance in Maine to rally support for a Republican senator who has bucked the Trump administration at key moments but remains critical to Republicans’ hopes of hanging onto the Senate majority.

The vice president offered up praise for Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is locked in a tight re-election battle, and made sure to tout her “independent” credentials when speaking at a manufacturing facility in Brewer.

“Whenever I’m in Maine, I got to give Susan a little bit of crap, because as you know, Susan is the most independent member of the United States Senate,” Vance said. “And as the president of the United States Senate, she sometimes makes my job just a little bit harder. But she makes it harder because she is coming to work every single day and fighting not for a political party or not for any abstraction; she comes to work every single day, and she fights for the great people of Maine.”

Collins, however, was not present at the rally, citing a scheduling conflict.

Collins’ absence and Vance’s emphasis on her voting record — she has frequently voted with the Trump administration but has opposed the president’s agenda at critical times — illustrates the uneasy relationship between the GOP senator and the White House in a state former Vice President Kamala Harris won by nearly 7 points in 2024.

And it demonstrates how they can be mutually beneficial to each other, with Vance appealing to the GOP base and Collins avoiding appearing alongside a prominent member of the Trump administration at a time when the president’s approval rating is underwater. Collins is set to face Democrat Troy Jackson in the November general election. Recent polling shows Jackson with a slight lead.

Over the weekend, Collins took aim at Trump’s trade war with Canada, which borders Maine.

“I really want us to go back to the very friendly, economically beneficial relationship that we have with our Canadian neighbors,” she told reporters, calling new tariffs “a mistake.”

Trump on Saturday escalated his trade war with the close American ally, imposing 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods after talks between the two nations collapsed. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney promised to retaliate “dollar for dollar” after walking away from what he characterized as a bad deal. And on Monday, Trump said the United States would impose 50% tariffs on all cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel from Canada beginning Jan. 1.“Build in the U.S. and there are ZERO TARIFFS. Canada will be treated like a State no longer!” he wrote in a post on X. “On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!”

At Monday’s rally, Vance defended the tariffs, calling Canada “a country that has underinvested in its military, that quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America.”

Vance initially referred to Canada as a U.S. state, which Trump has repeatedly done, but he insisted his remark was a “Freudian slip.”

“That was actually an accident,” the vice president said.

news.title: Steve Hilton Within Single Digits of Xavier Becerra in California—New Poll
news.text: Republican Steve Hilton has closed his deficit against Democrat Xavier Becerra to eight points in a new poll of California's governor race. Becerra leads Hilton 49.2 percent to 41 percent among 912 registered voters, with 9.8 percent undecided, according to the survey conducted August 14-16. The poll was commissioned by Hilton's campaign and conducted by David Wolfson, a pollster and faculty member in Columbia University's Political Analytics graduate program. It carries a 3.3-point margin of error and used MMS text-to-web methodology. Hilton seized on the numbers. “Xavier Becerra’s support is collapsing as more and more Californians learn about his horrific record as HHS secretary, which sent thousands of Latino kids into the clutches of child sex and labor traffickers,” Hilton told the California Post, which first reported the poll. Federal HHS oversight reports have documented gaps in sponsor screening and follow-up for unaccompanied migrant children, creating potential safety risks, but they do not establish Hilton's claim that HHS sent thousands of children into sex or labor trafficking. Newsweek reached out to the Hilton and Becerra campaigns for comment Monday. Becerra's Lead Holds Elsewhere The result stands out against a summer of consistent double-digit leads for Becerra. A University of California, Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll conducted August 3-9 among 2,310 likely voters in partnership with the Los Angeles Times found Becerra ahead 55 percent to 37 percent, an 18-point margin. “Today's poll is further confirmation that California voters support Secretary Becerra's focus on lowering the cost of living for California's working families and standing up against the hateful and disastrous policies pushed by Trump and his endorsed candidate, Steve Hilton,” Becerra's spokesperson Jonathan Underland responded to the Berkeley poll in a statement to Newsweek. A Public Policy Institute of California survey conducted June 29-July 6 put Becerra's lead at 25 points, 61 percent to 36 percent. A Kreate Strategies poll in mid-June found a similar 25-point gap. The gap between the Wolfson poll and other independent surveys is also reflected in prediction markets, which have barely moved despite the new poll. Polymarket has put Becerra's odds of winning in November at roughly 93 percent to 96 percent in recent weeks, compared with 3 percent to 4 percent for Hilton. Kalshi shows a similar spread, with Becerra near 96 percent and Hilton near 4 percent. An eight-model prediction aggregator run by OddsShopper put Becerra at 96.4 percent and Hilton at 3 percent. A Difficult Path for Hilton and the GOP Becerra and Hilton emerged from a contentious jungle primary in June and will face off in the November general election. Hilton, a former Fox News host and adviser to former British Prime Minister David Cameron, received Trump's endorsement in April. He has called the endorsement “a very powerful driver of turnout” heading into the midterm election. Becerra served as secretary of Health and Human Services during the Biden administration and previously served as California's attorney general and a member of Congress. But California remains a steep climb for any Republican. The last Republican to win the governorship was Arnold Schwarzenegger, the actor-turned-politician who won the 2003 recall election and was reelected in 2006. No Republican has won a statewide race in California since. Democrats have a nearly 2-to-1 registration advantage, while independents have favored Becerra by roughly 58 percent to 30 percent in Berkeley's polling. Trump's own performance in California has improved with each presidential election without coming close to winning the state. He won roughly 32 percent of the vote in 2016, 34 percent in 2020 and just over 38 percent in 2024. That trajectory is central to Hilton's argument that the governor's race should be decided on state issues rather than national politics, an argument Democrats have sought to counter by tying him closely to Trump. Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom cannot seek a third term, but Republicans still face an uphill battle in a state that remains one of the most Democratic in the country. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won California by 20 points in the 2024 presidential election, a narrower margin than former President Joe Biden's 29-point victory four years earlier. What Happens Next Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball don’t view the race as competitive, with both classifying it as safe or solid for Democrats. Polls will continue to be closely watched to gauge the mood of the electorate in California ahead of the November midterms. Hilton has challenged Becerra to a series of debates in the coming months, but it’s not clear when they will occur. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Cristina Diciu.
news.summary: Hilton has narrowed his deficit to Democrat Xavier Becerra to eight points, according to a new poll conducted by David Wolfson.

Below is State of the Day, a morning newsletter by Daily Caller Editor-at-Large Geoff Ingersoll. Sign up here.

Greetings, Dear Reader,

Welcome back to State of the Day, where I strip the euphemism and misdirection off national politics and give it to you straight, no ice, no mixer.

Let’s start off the week in fifth gear, shall we?

THERE ARE NOT ‘TWO SIDES’

The modern left cannot function without the Three E’s: euphemism, equivocation and false equivalence.

During a recent New York Times podcast, rising comedian and a member of the “Tires” cast on Netflix, Stavros Halkias said, “I don’t wanna do the both sides bullshit because it’s just not true. One side is worse than the other, objectively speaking. One side is disappearing people and one side wants children to have healthcare, I don’t think that’s equivalent.
